question: Under the previous rule, how long did staff have to use their lieu hours?
expected_answer: Overtime is compensated with time off within 16 weeks.
answer_text:
Under the overtime rule immediately preceding the current one, **POL-013-v1.5 (effective 2024-09-01)**, overtime was compensated with time off **within 16 weeks** [30]. The current POL-013-DE v2.0 (effective 2026-01-01) instead states **within 10 weeks** [31].

If you meant the earlier **FAQ-006 (effective 2024-02-01)** rather than POL-013-v1.5, it states time off **within 18 weeks** [14].

context_blocks.text: In most cases, a few days of notice is enough, but for longer breaks you should coordinate earlier with your team. If you join Kranich in the middle of the year, your bridge-day allowance is not pro-rated. You receive the full annual allowance regardless of when you start. If you leave Kranich during the year, no deduction is made for bridge days you have already taken. Bridge days are not considered when we calculate overtime or when we assess attendance for any purpose. They are a simple entitlement, and we trust you to use them sensibly.

5. Carryover

We want you to use your vacation within the calendar year. However, we know that plans change, and sometimes you cannot take all your days before December ends. Unused vacation days must be taken by March 15 of the following year. Days not taken by that date are forfeited.

If you have carryover days, you should schedule them early in the new year, before you plan new vacation. Your manager can help you find a good time, particularly if your team has seasonal peaks. People & Culture will send a reminder in January to anyone with a carryover balance.

Carryover is not paid out in cash at the end of the year. The purpose of the March 15 deadline is to ensure you actually take time off rather than accumulate days indefinitely. If exceptional circumstances prevent you from taking your days by the deadline, speak with your manager and People & Culture as early as possible; we will handle such cases individually and with care.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer working with clients in Poland, had three unused days at the end of December. He books them for early February, well before the March 15 deadline, and lets his clients know his availability in advance.

context_blocks.header: [4] POL-003-v1.0.pdf — Workation Guideline > 2. How much workation is allowed (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
2. How much workation is allowed

Workation is limited to 30 working days per calendar year within the EU/EEA. This means that, in any given calendar year, you may work from a location other than your usual place of employment for up to 30 working days in total. You do not need to take these days in one block; you can split them across several shorter stays, as long as the total does not exceed the yearly limit.

A single workation stay may not exceed 21 calendar days. If you wish to stay longer in a location, you would need to take regular leave or annual vacation for the remaining time, or arrange a different type of absence with your manager. The workation portion of your trip must fit within the 21 calendar days, and any additional days are your own time.

Please note that the limit applies to working days, while the maximum length of a single stay is counted in calendar days. For clarity, a stay that spans weekends or public holidays still counts toward the 21 calendar days, but only the working days within that stay count toward the 30 working days per calendar year.

Workation is available to all employees, regardless of your team or your home location. Whether you are a backend engineer in Lisbon, a customer success manager in Berlin, or a product manager working remotely from Spain, the same rules apply. You are responsible for tracking your own usage, and your manager will help you confirm that your plans fit within the limits before you go.

5. Carryover

We encourage you to use your full vacation entitlement within the calendar year. However, we understand that sometimes it is not possible, for example due to a heavy workload or an unexpected illness during your planned vacation.

Unused vacation days must be taken by March 31 of the following year. This means that if you do not use all of your vacation days by the end of the calendar year, you can carry them over into the next year, but you must use them by March 31 of that next year. Days not taken by that date are forfeited.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, has three unused vacation days at the end of the year. She carries them over and takes a long weekend in early March of the following year, well before the March 31 deadline.

If you are unable to take your carried-over days by March 31 because of a documented illness or another exceptional circumstance, please speak with your manager and People & Culture. We will handle such situations individually and with flexibility.

Wo diese Richtlinie großzügiger ist als lokale Regelungen, gilt die Richtlinie. Wo lokale Regelungen mehr verlangen, gelten die lokalen Regelungen. 2. How much workation is allowed

Workation is limited to 30 working days per calendar year within the EU/EEA. This means you can spend up to 30 working days per year working from another EU/EEA country, in addition to any remote work you already do within your home country under POL-002.

FAQ Elternzeit

1. Questions **When does overtime apply?**  
Overtime applies when your manager asks you to work beyond your regular contracted hours. Occasional extra minutes to finish a task do not count as overtime. We expect overtime to be the exception, not the rule, and to be balanced with rest. **Do I need approval before working overtime?**  
Yes. Please agree overtime with your manager in advance, either in person or in writing. If an urgent situation arises, notify your manager as soon as possible, ideally before you start the extra work. For guidance on requesting and recording overtime, see POL-004. **How do I record overtime?**  
Record your overtime in Fern, our HRIS, in the same place you log your regular working time. Your manager will confirm the entry. If you have questions about how to enter the time, reach out to people@kranich.example or your local People & Culture contact. **How is overtime compensated?**  
Overtime is compensated with time off within 18 weeks. You take the time off at a mutually convenient moment with your manager, considering team workload and client commitments. The aim is to take the time off before it expires, so please plan it early rather than waiting until the end of the period. **Can I receive overtime as extra pay instead?**  
In most cases, no. Our policy is time off in lieu, which supports sustainable work habits. Exceptions are rare and only considered where local law or a specific contract requires payment. If you believe an exception applies, speak with your manager, who will involve People & Culture. **What if I cannot take the time off within 18 weeks?**  
If you have not been able to take your overtime as time off within 18 weeks, talk to your manager promptly. Together you will find a solution, for example by planning the time off in the next scheduling cycle. Please do not let the time accumulate silently; we want you to rest. **What about overtime during travel or client visits?**  
Time spent traveling for work, outside your regular hours, counts as overtime when your manager has approved it in advance.

1. Questions **How much vacation do I get?** Full-time employees receive 25 days of vacation per calendar year. This is the standard entitlement for everyone employed on a full-time basis, regardless of which office or country you work from. Part-time employees receive a pro-rated amount based on their contracted hours. **When does my vacation year run?** Our vacation year is the calendar year. You can book vacation days for the current year at any time, and you should plan to use them within that same year. Please check POL-004 for the rules on carrying days over to the next year. **How do I request vacation?** Submit your request through Fern, our HRIS. Choose the dates you want, add a short note for your manager, and send it for approval. Your manager will review it promptly. If you need to change or cancel an approved request, you can do so in Fern as long as your manager has not already approved the change. **Who approves my vacation?** Your direct manager approves vacation requests. They will consider team coverage and business needs when making a decision. We encourage you to discuss your plans with your team early, especially if you are requesting popular dates such as school holidays or the period between Christmas and New Year. **What if I am sick during my vacation?** If you fall ill while on vacation, you can report your sickness through the usual process in Fern. You will not lose the vacation days for the period you were sick. Please let your manager know as soon as possible and follow the sickness reporting steps described in POL-004. **Can I take vacation in my first months with the company?** Yes. Vacation accrues from your first day of employment. You can request days once you have started, even if you joined recently. Your manager will help you plan around your onboarding and any initial training. **What about public holidays?** Public holidays are separate from your vacation days. They depend on the country where you work and, in Germany, on the federal state of your workplace. Public holidays do not reduce your vacation entitlement. **Where can I find more details?** The full policy is available in POL-004 on Grove.

context_blocks.header: [16] POL-001-v1.0.pdf — Vacation & Leave Policy > 6. Special leave (p. 2–3)
context_blocks.text:
6. Special leave

Beyond annual vacation, Kranich offers special leave for certain life events. You do not need to use your vacation days for these situations. Special leave is paid and does not reduce your vacation balance.

•  Bereavement leave. If a close family member passes away, you may take a few days of paid leave to attend to arrangements and to grieve. Your manager and People & Culture are available to support you. •  Care leave. If a dependent falls ill or needs urgent care, you may take a short period of paid leave to manage the situation. For longer care arrangements, please talk to People & Culture about options. •  Moving day. When you move house, you may take a day of paid leave to handle the move. This applies once per move. •  Medical appointments. Routine medical appointments that cannot be scheduled outside working hours do not count as vacation. Please inform your manager in advance. •  Public duties. If you serve on a jury or are called for civic duties, you may take paid leave for the required time.

Special leave is requested through Fern using the appropriate category. If you are unsure whether your situation qualifies, ask People & Culture. We trust you to use this leave responsibly, and we will never ask for intrusive details about your personal circumstances.

Example: Lea, a people operations specialist in Berlin, takes a day of special leave when she moves to a new apartment across town. She submits the request in Fern the week before and spends the day unpacking without checking work email.

context_blocks.header: [19] POL-001-v2.3.pdf — Vacation & Leave Policy > 3. Annual vacation entitlement (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
3. Annual vacation entitlement

Full-time employees receive 27 days of vacation per calendar year. This entitlement is calculated on a pro-rata basis for part-time employees, based on the number of hours you work per week. For example, if you work half-time, your annual vacation entitlement is half of the full- time amount.

Tenure adds one day per two full years of service, up to a total of 30 days. This means that after two full years with Kranich, you earn an additional vacation day, and after four full years you earn another one, and so on. The maximum total vacation entitlement, including tenure days, is 30 days per calendar year. Your tenure is counted from your start date as an employee, and the additional days take effect at the beginning of the calendar year following the anniversary of your start date.

You accrue vacation days throughout the calendar year. Your entitlement for a given year is available in full at the start of that year, but if you join or leave Kranich mid-year, your entitlement is adjusted pro-rata. New employees who join during the first half of the year receive the full annual entitlement; those who join in the second half receive a pro-rata amount.

Vacation days are intended for rest and personal time. You do not need to provide a reason for taking vacation, and we do not require you to document how you spend your time off.

context_blocks.header: [20] POL-001-v2.0.pdf — Vacation & Leave Policy > 6. Special leave (p. 2–3)
context_blocks.text:
6. Special leave

In addition to annual vacation, you may be eligible for special leave in certain circumstances. Special leave is paid time off for events that require you to be away from work for a short period. It is separate from your annual vacation entitlement and does not reduce the days you have for vacation.

Examples of special leave include moving to a new home, attending a close family member's wedding, or dealing with a sudden personal matter. You may also take special leave for important appointments that cannot be scheduled outside working hours, such as a visa

appointment or a legal hearing.

Special leave is granted at the discretion of your manager and the People & Culture team. The amount of time depends on the situation; we ask you to be reasonable and to keep your manager informed. For most situations, a day or two is sufficient, and longer arrangements should be discussed with People & Culture.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer who works with clients in Poland, needs to attend his sister's wedding on a Thursday. He speaks with his manager, who approves one day of special leave. Marek uses the day for the wedding and schedules his client visits around it.

To request special leave, submit a request in Fern and select the appropriate leave type. Your manager will approve it if the circumstances qualify. If you are unsure whether your situation counts as special leave, ask People & Culture before you make plans.

5. Carryover

We encourage you to use your full annual vacation entitlement within the calendar year. Taking regular breaks supports your wellbeing and prevents burnout.

Unused vacation days must be taken by March 31 of the following year. In other words, if you have days left over at the end of December, you may carry them into the new year, but you must use them by the end of March. Days not taken by that date are forfeited.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, had a busy autumn and did not use all of her vacation days by the end of the year. She carries the remaining days into the new year and books them for a long weekend in February. Because she uses them before March 31, she loses nothing.

If you know early in the year that you will not be able to use all of your days, talk to your manager. Sometimes a different schedule or a shorter break can help. The goal is that everyone takes the time they are entitled to.

context_blocks.header: [23] POL-004-v2.0.pdf — Travel & Expense Policy > 6. Submitting expenses (p. 3)
context_blocks.text:
6. Submitting expenses

Submit your expense report in Ledgerly after your trip. Expense reports are due within 45 calendar days after the trip ends. This timeline helps Finance close the books accurately and ensures you get reimbursed promptly.

For each expense, attach a receipt unless the expense is covered by the per-diem. Receipts must show the date, the vendor, and the amount. If a receipt is missing, explain why in the report; we understand that sometimes a receipt is lost.

Group your expenses by trip and by category. Ledgerly will guide you through the steps. When you submit, your manager will receive a notification to approve the report. After approval, Finance processes the reimbursement through payroll or bank transfer, depending on your location.

If you have an advance for the trip, you must settle it in the same report. Any unused advance must be returned with the report, and any shortfall will be added to your reimbursement.

If you submit late, we may still process your report, but we ask you to explain the delay. Repeated late submissions may affect how quickly we can reimburse you.

Example: Deniz returns from her client visit in Hamburg on a Thursday. The following week, she opens Ledgerly, attaches her train ticket and hotel receipt, claims the per-diem for her two travel days, and submits the report. Her manager approves it within a few days, and Finance reimburses her in the next payroll cycle.

7. Questions

If you have questions about this policy, start with your manager. For questions about a specific expense, contact Finance through Ledgerly. For questions about how this policy interacts with your employment contract or local law, contact People & Culture at people@kranich.example.

We also encourage you to flag anything that feels unclear or unfair. This policy is meant to support you, not to create barriers. Your feedback helps us improve it.

Doc Id: POL-001-v1.0 · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2023-01-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose

Kranich Software GmbH wants everyone to take time to rest, recharge and attend to personal matters. This policy explains how vacation works at Kranich, how to request time off, and what happens when you have unused days at the end of the year. We believe that planned, regular time away from work makes for healthier colleagues and better products.

2. Scope

This policy applies to all employees of Kranich Software GmbH, regardless of whether you work from our office in Berlin, our office in Lisbon, or remotely from your home in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France or the United Kingdom. It covers vacation entitlement, the request process, carryover rules and special leave. If you are employed through a local entity in one of our countries of operation, the statutory minimums of that country apply as a floor; where this policy is more generous, this policy governs.

3. Annual vacation entitlement

Full-time employees receive 24 days of vacation per calendar year. This entitlement is prorated for part-time employees and for those who join or leave Kranich partway through the year. Your entitlement is calculated based on the number of months you are employed during the calendar year, and People & Culture will confirm your individual balance in Fern when you start and at the beginning of each year.

Vacation days are counted as full working days. If you work a reduced schedule, your days are counted proportionally. You accrue vacation throughout the year, but you may request days before the full entitlement has accrued, as long as the request is reasonable and your team can plan around it.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, joined Kranich in the middle of the year. Her entitlement for her first calendar year is prorated to reflect the months she is employed, and she can see her exact balance in Fern.

Working Time & Overtime Policy

Superseded by version 2.0.

1. Purpose

This policy explains how we think about working time at Kranich Software GmbH. We want everyone to do meaningful work without burning out, and we know that clear expectations help with that. The policy applies to all employees in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France and the United Kingdom, regardless of whether you usually work from home, from one of our offices in Berlin or Lisbon, or at a client site.

context_blocks.header: [26] POL-001-DE.pdf — Urlaubs- und Abwesenheitsrichtlinie > 4. Beantragung von Urlaub (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
4. Beantragung von Urlaub

Zur Beantragung von Urlaub reichen Sie eine Anfrage über Fern, unser HRIS, ein. Ihre Führungskraft erhält eine Benachrichtigung und kann die Anfrage genehmigen oder ablehnen. Bitte reichen Sie Ihre Anfrage so früh wie möglich ein, damit Ihr Team Ihre Abwesenheit einplanen kann.

Anfragen für mehr als fünf aufeinanderfolgende Tage müssen 4 Wochen im Voraus eingereicht werden. Diese Vorlaufzeit hilft Ihrem Team, die Vertretung zu planen, und stellt sicher, dass kundenorientierte Arbeit reibungslos weiterläuft. Bei kürzeren Anfragen bitten wir Sie, Ihrer Führungskraft zumindest ein paar Tage Vorlauf zu geben, auch wenn wir verstehen, dass sich Pläne manchmal kurzfristig ändern.

Wenn Sie Urlaub beantragen, berücksichtigt Ihre Führungskraft die Bedürfnisse des Teams und die Arbeitsbelastung zu diesem Zeitpunkt. Wir bemühen uns, alle Anfragen zu genehmigen, können Anfragen jedoch ablehnen oder um eine Verschiebung bitten, wenn zu viele Teammitglieder gleichzeitig abwesend sind oder ein wichtiger Termin bevorsteht. Wird Ihre Anfrage abgelehnt, erklärt Ihre Führungskraft den Grund und hilft Ihnen, ein alternatives Datum zu finden.

Beispiel: Marek, ein Field Solutions Engineer, der mit Kundinnen und Kunden in Polen arbeitet, möchte im Sommer eine Woche freinehmen. Er reicht seine Anfrage vier Wochen im Voraus über Fern ein, und seine Führungskraft genehmigt sie, nachdem sie bestätigt hat, dass in dieser Woche keine Kundenworkshops geplant sind.

Wenn Sie eine genehmigte Urlaubsanfrage ändern oder stornieren müssen, aktualisieren Sie die Anfrage bitte so bald wie möglich in Fern, damit Ihr Team seine Pläne anpassen kann.

7. Fragen

Wenn Sie Fragen zu dieser Richtlinie haben, wenden Sie sich bitte an People & Culture unter people@kranich.example. Bei Fragen zur Erfassung von Abwesenheiten in Fern kontaktieren Sie bitte den IT-Support unter it-help@kranich.example. Wir helfen Ihnen gerne, Ihre Ansprüche und das Verfahren zur Beantragung von Freizeit zu verstehen.

Wir überprüfen diese Richtlinie regelmäßig und können sie von Zeit zu Zeit aktualisieren. Wenn wir Änderungen vornehmen, kommunizieren wir diese über Grove, unser Intranet, und aktualisieren entsprechend die Richtlinienversion. Die auf Grove veröffentlichte Version ist stets die aktuellste.

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose

This policy explains how vacation works at Kranich Software GmbH. We believe that time away from work helps everyone return refreshed and do their best work. This policy sets out your annual vacation entitlement, how to request time off, and what happens to unused days at the end of the year.

We keep the process simple. You request vacation through Fern, our human resources system, and your manager approves it. We trust each other to plan ahead so that teams can cover important work while you are away.

2. Scope

This policy applies to all employees of Kranich Software GmbH, regardless of whether you work from our Berlin office in Ritterstraße, our Lisbon office in Rua do Alecrim, or remotely from your home in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France, or the United Kingdom. We are a remote-first company, and this policy treats everyone the same no matter where they are employed.

The policy covers annual vacation entitlement, the request process, carryover of unused days, and special leave. It does not cover sick leave, parental leave, or other statutory leave types; those are handled separately and you can find more information in the relevant policies on Grove, our intranet.

context_blocks.header: [30] POL-013-v1.5.pdf — Working Time & Overtime Policy > 3. Overtime and compensation (p. 2)
context_blocks.text: 3. Overtime and compensation Overtime is any time you work beyond your individually agreed weekly hours, up to the weekly limit in §2. Overtime is not routine. It happens when there is a genuine spike in workload, a critical incident, a client deadline, or another exceptional situation. Your manager should know about overtime before or shortly after it occurs. You should not work overtime just because a colleague does, and you should not feel pressure to work longer to appear committed. If you feel that expectation, tell your manager or contact People & Culture. We evaluate performance on outcomes, not on hours. Overtime is compensated with time off within 16 weeks. This means that when you work extra hours, you should take an equivalent amount of time off during the following sixteen weeks, at a time that suits you and your team. Time off in lieu is the primary form of compensation for overtime across Kranich, and it applies to all employees covered by this policy. You do not need to submit a formal request for overtime compensation in advance. Instead, agree with your manager on a day or half-day to take off, and record it in Fern as you would any other time off. If you have accumulated overtime but have not been able to take the time off within the sixteen-week window, talk to your manager. Together you will find a way to clear the balance promptly, for example by scheduling the time off before the window closes. Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, works an extra two hours one evening to support a client during a critical migration. The following week, she leaves early on a Thursday afternoon and records the two hours as time off in Fern. Her manager approves it, and her overtime balance is cleared. Overtime during on-call duty is handled separately. If you are on call, you are compensated for being reachable, and any actual work you perform while on call counts as working time and is subject to the same time-off compensation described above. Your team lead can explain the on-call arrangements that apply to your role. We do not pay overtime as additional salary. The time-off model keeps things simple and fair, and it protects your rest.

context_blocks.header: [31] POL-013-DE.pdf — Arbeitszeit- und Überstundenrichtlinie > 3. Überstunden und Ausgleich (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text: 3. Überstunden und Ausgleich Überstunden sind Arbeitszeiten über Ihre regelmäßigen vertraglichen Stunden hinaus, die auf Veranlassung Ihrer Führungskraft oder mit deren Zustimmung geleistet werden. Gelegentliche Überstunden können in unserem Geschäft vorkommen, zum Beispiel rund um einen Produktstart oder wenn ein Kunde ein dringendes Problem hat. Sie sollten die Ausnahme bleiben, nicht die Regel. Von Ihnen wird niemals erwartet, regelmäßig Überstunden zu leisten. Wenn Überstunden häufig vorkommen, sollte Ihre Führungskraft die Situation prüfen und Prioritäten oder Ressourcen anpassen. Lange Arbeitszeiten über einen längeren Zeitraum sind weder für Sie, noch für Ihr Team oder die Qualität unserer Arbeit gut. Überstunden werden durch Freizeit innerhalb von 10 Wochen ausgeglichen. Das bedeutet: Wenn Sie zusätzliche Stunden arbeiten, sollten Sie bald danach eine entsprechende Menge an Freizeit nehmen, damit die zusätzliche Anstrengung zeitnah ausgeglichen wird. Die Freizeit wird in Absprache mit Ihrer Führungskraft genommen und sollte Ihr Team oder Ihre Kunden nicht beeinträchtigen. Sie müssen Überstunden nicht in einem speziellen System erfassen. Informieren Sie einfach Ihre Führungskraft, wenn Sie zusätzliche Stunden arbeiten, und vereinbaren Sie gemeinsam, wann Sie den entsprechenden Freizeitausgleich nehmen. Wenn Sie möchten, können Sie es in Ihrem Kalender oder in einer Nachricht an Ihre Führungskraft notieren. Freizeitausgleich soll genutzt werden. Bitte lassen Sie ihn nicht anwachsen. Wenn Sie ausstehenden Freizeitausgleich haben und es schwierig finden, ihn zu planen, hilft Ihnen Ihre Führungskraft, einen guten Zeitpunkt zu finden. In jedem Fall sollte der Freizeitausgleich innerhalb des oben genannten Zeitraums genommen werden. Beispiel: Deniz, Customer Success Managerin in Berlin, arbeitet eines Abends ein paar zusätzliche Stunden, um einem Kunden bei einem Konfigurationsproblem zu helfen. Sie erwähnt es am nächsten Tag gegenüber ihrer Führungskraft, und gemeinsam vereinbaren sie, dass sie am Freitag der darauffolgenden Woche früher Schluss macht. Überstunden werden nicht in Geld vergütet. Wir glauben, dass Freizeit die wertvollste Form des Ausgleichs ist, weil sie Ihre Erholung und Ihr Leben außerhalb der Arbeit unterstützt.

3. Vacation

Employees in Germany receive 27 days of statutory-plus-Kranich vacation per year. This is your full annual entitlement, calculated on a calendar-year basis. You accrue your vacation entitlement pro rata for each full month of employment in a given year.

You plan your vacation in Fern. Please submit your request as early as you can, and at least a

few weeks before your planned leave, so your team can plan around your absence. Your manager approves or declines your request. We ask that you do not take all your vacation at once; spread it across the year so you and your team stay rested.

Vacation should be taken within the calendar year. If you cannot take all your vacation due to operational reasons or illness, you may carry it over into the first quarter of the following year. Unused vacation from previous years expires in line with German law unless your manager has explicitly agreed to a carryover in writing.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, is employed in Germany. She plans a two-week trip to visit family in the autumn. She submits her request in Fern in early summer, her manager approves it, and her team coordinates coverage. Anna still has several days left for the winter holidays.

If you leave Kranich, your accrued but unused vacation will be paid out in your final salary, or you will take it during your notice period, depending on what your manager and People & Culture agree with you. For questions about your vacation balance, write to people@kranich.example.

context_blocks.header: [33] HR-LEAVE.pdf — Leave Administration Guide > 3. Process > Review and approval (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
Review and approval

Your manager receives your request in Fern and reviews it. They will consider the needs of the team, the time of year, and any other requests already approved. Your manager may approve the request directly or reach out to discuss it first.

You will receive a notification in Fern once a decision is made. If your request is declined, your manager will explain why and help you find an alternative.

Cancelling or changing a request

If your plans change, update your request in Fern as soon as you know. Cancel or modify the

dates so your manager and team have accurate information. There is no penalty for changing a request, but please be considerate of others who may be planning around you.

Handover

Before you go on leave, agree with your manager on a handover. This is especially important for longer absences. Let your team know what you are working on and who to contact in your absence. A short note in your team channel is often enough.

Returning to work

When you return, check in with your manager and your team. Catch up on anything you missed and pick up your tasks again. Your first day back is a good time to review your inbox and any messages in team channels.

4. Timelines

We aim to keep the process simple and predictable.

•  Submit your request through Fern as early as possible. •  Your manager reviews requests promptly. •  You will receive a decision in Fern once your manager has responded.

For leave around busy periods, such as the end of the year, submit earlier than usual. This helps your team plan fairly when several people want time off at the same time.

If you need to take leave at short notice, for example due to a family matter, speak to your manager directly. They can help you arrange the time you need without waiting for the usual process.

Some types of leave follow different timelines. Your manager or the People & Culture team can point you to the right information. For example, the parental carryover exception lives in POL-008 §7, which explains how parental leave interacts with your leave balance.

context_blocks.header: [34] POL-001-v2.0.pdf — Vacation & Leave Policy > 3. Annual vacation entitlement (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
3. Annual vacation entitlement

Full-time employees receive 25 days of vacation per calendar year. This entitlement is for the calendar year, which runs from January through December, matching our fiscal year.

If you join Kranich Software partway through the year, your entitlement is calculated proportionally based on the months remaining in the calendar year. If you leave the company partway through the year, you are expected to use vacation days in proportion to the time you have worked; any days taken beyond that proportion will be deducted from your final pay.

Part-time employees receive vacation on a pro-rata basis. For example, if you work half of a full-time schedule, you would receive half of the annual entitlement. Your exact entitlement is visible in Fern, and the People & Culture team can help you understand how it is calculated for your specific working pattern.

Vacation days are counted in full days. If you normally work a partial day, you should discuss with your manager how to account for vacation time in a way that is fair and consistent.

This does not apply to damage caused by gross negligence; such cases are handled individually. **Can I request additional equipment during my employment?**
Yes. If your needs change — for example, you move to a role that requires more screen space — submit a request through the channel described in POL-004. We review requests regularly and aim to respond promptly. **Example:** Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, needed a second monitor after starting to review code reviews more frequently. She submitted a request through the standard process and received it within a few days. **What about equipment for visitors or contractors?**
Visitors and short-term contractors use loaner equipment from the office. For longer engagements, the responsible manager arranges dedicated equipment following the same process. **Where can I find the full equipment policy?**
See POL-004 for the complete policy, including eligibility and the replacement schedule. For travel-related equipment questions, refer to FIN-RATES-2026.

Flexible Working Requests

1. Purpose

At Kranich Software, we know that people do their best work when they can shape their day around their lives. Flexible working is part of how we work, and this policy explains how you can request a change to your working pattern, when you can expect an answer, and what happens after a request is approved.

Flexible working can mean many things: adjusting your start and end times, working from home on certain days, or changing the distribution of your hours across the week. It is not limited to parents or carers — anyone can ask, whatever their reason. We trust you to make a case that works for you and for your team.

2. Who this is for

This policy applies to all employees in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France and the United Kingdom, regardless of where you usually sit — at the Ritterstraße office in Berlin, the Rua do Alecrim office in Lisbon, or remotely from home.

Some teams, such as Routing Core or Platform & Infrastructure, have on-call or release responsibilities. Others, like Customer Success, need to cover client hours. Your role and your team's commitments will shape what is possible, but they should not stop you from asking.

If you are a manager, you will be involved in the conversation as a supporter, not a gatekeeper. If you are an employee, this policy is written for you.

7. Questions

If you have any questions about this policy, please reach out to People & Culture at people@kranich.example. For questions about how to record leave in Fern, please contact IT support at it-help@kranich.example. We are happy to help you understand your entitlements and the process for requesting time off.

We review this policy regularly and may update it from time to time. When we make changes, we will communicate them through Grove, our intranet, and update the policy version accordingly. The version published on Grove is always the most current one.

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose

This policy explains how vacation and other leave work at Kranich Software GmbH. We believe that taking time away from work helps everyone recharge, stay healthy, and do their best work. This version supersedes version 2.0, which was published earlier. We updated the policy to make the rules clearer and to reflect how we work across our offices in Berlin and Lisbon, as well as remotely. If anything in this policy conflicts with a local legal requirement in the country where you are employed, the local requirement takes precedence. Please reach out to People & Culture if you have questions about how this policy applies to you.

2. Scope

This policy applies to all employees of Kranich Software GmbH, regardless of whether you work from our Berlin office, our Lisbon office, or remotely from your home in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France, or the United Kingdom. It covers vacation entitlement, how to request time off, carryover rules, and special leave situations. Contractors, interns, and temporary workers are not covered by this policy; their arrangements are handled separately by their engagement contracts.

question: According to the latest update, how many minutes are our morning meetings limited to?
expected_answer: Daily standups are capped at 14 minutes.
answer_text:
The context does not use the term "morning meetings"; the closest and relevant limit is on daily standups, which is what the meeting notes cap.

Latest dated update: MTG-04 (2025-05-13) decides that daily standups are capped at 14 minutes [16]. For comparison, the earlier MTG-03 (2025-04-10) set a cap of 17 minutes [38].

If by "morning meetings" you mean something other than the daily standups covered in MTG-04/MTG-03, that is not available in the supplied context.

context_blocks.text:
5. Questions

We encourage you to question the meetings you are invited to. If you believe your presence is not needed, decline the invitation with a polite note — this is not rudeness, it is respect for everyone's time. If you believe a meeting lacks purpose or an agenda, say so to the host before

the meeting, not during it.

We also encourage you to question meetings you host. After a meeting, ask yourself: did we need it? Did we achieve what we set out to do? Could it have been an email, a document, or a recording? If the answer leans toward "no" or "yes, it could have been async," change the approach next time.

If you feel that a recurring meeting has outlived its usefulness, raise it. Propose cancelling it, reducing its frequency, or changing its format. The person who called the meeting into question is doing the whole company a favour.

For questions about this guideline, or for help designing a better meeting practice for your team, reach out to your manager or the Leadership Team. For practical support with scheduling tools or calendar settings, contact it-help@kranich.example. For anything related to how we work together as people, people@kranich.example is always open.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer working with clients in Poland, receives an invitation to a weekly internal status call. He checks the agenda and realises the update is already covered in the shared project tracker. He declines politely, noting that he will flag anything urgent directly. The host thanks him — one fewer attendee makes the call shorter for everyone else.

We trust you to use this guideline with good sense. Meetings are not the enemy; thoughtless meetings are. Protect your focus, respect your colleagues' time, and keep the conversation going — async first, synchronous when it matters.

5. Questions

If you have questions about this guideline, start with your manager or your team lead. For practical questions about scheduling tools or calendar settings, contact it- help@kranich.example. For questions about how this policy interacts with other policies, such

as POL-004 on remote work, reach out to people@kranich.example and we will point you to the right owner.

If you believe a meeting you attend is unnecessary, wasteful, or poorly facilitated, say so constructively — to the facilitator or to your manager. We would rather hear about a problem than let it persist. Similarly, if you notice that a recurring meeting has drifted from its purpose, propose canceling it or changing its format.

The Leadership Team reviews this guideline periodically. We welcome suggestions for improvement from anyone at Kranich, whether you work from the Berlin office, the Lisbon office, or remotely from another country. Send your ideas to people@kranich.example, and we will consider them in the next review cycle.

Example: Lea, a people operations specialist in Berlin, receives a question from a new colleague about whether they may schedule a meeting during focus time for an urgent client call. Lea explains the rule, then offers an alternative: the colleague can ask the client to move the call, or if that is impossible, they can request an exception from their manager. The guideline is firm, but it is not rigid — we trust people to use judgment in rare situations.

Meetings are a tool for collaboration, not a substitute for it. By protecting focus time, keeping decision rooms small, and defaulting to asynchronous work, we give each other the space to do our best work. Thank you for helping us keep meetings meaningful.

context_blocks.header: [3] POL-020-v1.0.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 3. Running a good meeting (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Running a good meeting

A good meeting starts before it begins. Every meeting must have a clear purpose and an agenda shared in advance, even if the agenda is just a few bullet points. If you cannot articulate why the meeting exists, it probably should not. If you are invited to a meeting without an agenda, ask the host for one — or ask whether the meeting can happen without you.

Keep the attendee list small. Invite people who need to contribute or decide, and include others only if they will benefit from hearing the discussion. You can always share notes afterward with people who were not in the room. As a rule of thumb, if you find yourself wondering why someone is on the invitation, have the conversation about removing them — kindly.

Start on time and end on time. Late starts punish punctual people, and overruns bleed into everyone else's day. If you finish early, end early. There is no virtue in filling the remaining minutes.

Assign a note-taker before the meeting starts. Notes should capture decisions, action items, and owners — not a transcript. At the end of the meeting, take a moment to recap decisions and confirm who does what next. If no action items or decisions emerged, consider whether the meeting needed to happen at all.

For recurring meetings, review the series every few months. Ask yourselves: is this still serving us? Would an async update or a shorter cadence work? Cancelling a recurring meeting is a sign of health, not failure.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, hosts a weekly check-in with a client. She notices that most weeks, the client has nothing new to share and the meeting runs on pleasantries. She proposes moving to a monthly call with a written update in between. The client agrees, and Deniz uses the reclaimed time to prepare a deeper quarterly review.

context_blocks.header: [4] POL-020-v1.1.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 3. Running a good meeting (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Running a good meeting

Every meeting should have a clear purpose and a named facilitator. The facilitator is responsible for the agenda, the pace, and the outcome. If a meeting lacks an agenda, the facilitator should cancel it or send one promptly.

Decision meetings are capped at 6 people. This limit keeps discussions sharp and ensures that everyone present can genuinely contribute. If a decision affects a wider group, the facilitator shares the outcome afterward and invites feedback within a reasonable window rather than

expanding the room.

Before you schedule a meeting, ask yourself: what do we need to achieve, and who truly needs to be in the room? Invite people because they can contribute to the outcome, not because they might be interested. You can always share notes with people who are not invited.

For recurring meetings, review the attendee list and the agenda at least once per quarter. Cancel sessions that no longer serve a purpose. It is better to end a recurring meeting early than to let it drift.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, wants to discuss a client escalation with Marek, a field solutions engineer in Poland, and Sofia, a product manager in Fleet Insights in Spain. Deniz keeps the meeting to the three of them plus herself, because the decision does not require anyone else. Afterward, she posts a short summary in Grove for the wider Customer Success team.

Meeting hygiene matters. Start on time, end on time, and allocate a minute or two at the end to confirm next steps and owners. If you are running late or must leave early, say so at the start. If you are attending remotely, join from a quiet space and mute yourself when you are not speaking.

context_blocks.header: [6] POL-020-v1.0.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 2. Focus time (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
2. Focus time

Deep work is the foundation of our craft. Writing code, analysing data, designing a solution, or preparing a customer workshop all require stretches of uninterrupted concentration. Constant context switching fragments our thinking and lowers the quality of everything we do.

To protect this, every weekday afternoon holds 2 hours of company-wide focus time with no meetings. During this window, you will not receive meeting invitations, and we ask you not to schedule any. This applies to all teams and all locations, including customer-facing roles. If a customer requests a meeting during focus time, offer an alternative slot the same day or the next working day; in urgent situations, speak with your manager first.

Focus time is not a break — it is working time, and you are still expected to be reachable for urgent matters through your usual channels. If something genuinely cannot wait, send a direct message rather than scheduling a meeting. We trust you to use your judgment about what counts as urgent.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, uses focus time to work through a complex routing algorithm. Her colleague in Berlin knows not to invite her to a sync during that window and instead leaves a thoughtful comment on the pull request. Anna picks it up when her focus block ends.

Meeting Culture Guideline

1. Purpose

Meetings are a means to an end: they help us align, decide, and move work forward. At Kranich Software GmbH, we also know that meetings cost us something precious — the uninterrupted time we need to build great software and support our customers. This guideline sets out how we plan, run, and question meetings so that they serve us rather than the other way around.

This policy applies to everyone at Kranich, whether you work from the Ritterstraße office in Berlin, the Rua do Alecrim office in Lisbon, or remotely from your home in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France, or the United Kingdom. It covers internal meetings as well as meetings with customers and partners, though we always apply good judgment when an external party expects a more formal rhythm.

We believe that a healthy meeting culture is a shared responsibility. Meeting hosts own the agenda and the outcome. Attendees own their presence and their contribution. And every one of us owns the courage to decline an invitation that does not need us.

context_blocks.header: [10] POL-013-v1.5.pdf — Working Time & Overtime Policy > 2. Working time (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
2. Working time

Working time is the time you spend performing your duties for Kranich. It includes your regular work, client calls, internal meetings, and time spent on business travel during what would otherwise be your working hours. It does not include your lunch break, other unpaid breaks, or your commute between home and the office.

Our standard working week runs from Monday to Friday. We do not prescribe fixed start and end times; you and your manager agree on a schedule that fits your team's collaboration needs and your personal circumstances. What matters is that you are available for the meetings and tasks your role requires, and that you coordinate with colleagues across time zones.

Working time may not exceed 44 hours in any week. This limit includes overtime. We count a week from Monday to Sunday. If you work in a jurisdiction with a stricter weekly limit, the stricter limit applies to you.

We expect you to take breaks during the day. A break of at least thirty minutes is recommended when you work more than six hours. You should also take time away from the screen regularly; short walks or stretching count as breaks only if they are not part of your duties.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, usually starts at nine and finishes around five- thirty. On a week with a late deployment, she works until seven on two evenings. She keeps an eye on her total so that she stays under the weekly limit.

If you regularly need more than the standard hours to complete your work, speak with your manager. That is usually a sign that priorities need adjusting or that the team needs more support, not that you should work longer. We do not expect anyone to answer messages outside their agreed working hours, unless they are on call or have explicitly agreed otherwise

with their team.

context_blocks.header: [11] POL-020-v1.1.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 2. Focus time (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
2. Focus time

Deep work requires uninterrupted stretches of time. We protect that time deliberately. Every weekday afternoon holds 2 hours of company-wide focus time with no meetings. During those hours, you can decline any meeting invitation without explanation, and you should not expect an immediate reply to messages.

Focus time is not a break. It is a shared commitment to let each other think. If you are in the Ritterstraße office in Berlin or the Rua do Alecrim office in Lisbon, treat focus time as quiet time in shared spaces. If you work from home, let your household know that a call is unlikely.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Routing Core in Lisbon, uses focus time to reason through a complex routing constraint. She knows her colleagues in Berlin will not schedule a call during that window, so she can safely block the time in her calendar as busy.

If you need additional focus beyond the company-wide window, you are welcome to mark your calendar as busy. The default expectation is that you will be available for meetings outside the protected window, but occasional blocks for deep work are normal and healthy.

context_blocks.header: [12] POL-020-v1.1.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 4. Async first (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
4. Async first

Asynchronous communication is our default. We work across time zones from Berlin to Lisbon and beyond, and we do not assume that everyone can attend a live call at a moment’s notice. Write things down, share them in Grove or the appropriate channel, and let people respond when they are able.

Use a meeting only when a live conversation adds value: brainstorming that benefits from rapid back-and-forth, resolving a conflict, or making a decision that requires discussion rather than a simple vote. For everything else, prefer documents, recorded updates, or written questions.

When you share a document for feedback, state the deadline for comments clearly and name the decision owner. If you need an answer, ask a direct question rather than posting a document and hoping for replies.

Example: Sofia, a product manager in Fleet Insights working remotely from Spain, wants input on a proposed change to how we present fleet health scores. Instead of scheduling a call with several stakeholders, she writes a short proposal, posts it in the Fleet Insights channel, and asks for comments by the end of the week. Colleagues in Poland and the United Kingdom respond asynchronously, and Sofia incorporates their feedback before the next team sync.

If you schedule a meeting, share the agenda and any pre-read material at least a day in advance. Do not use meeting time for silent reading. If attendees have not had a chance to read the material, consider rescheduling or summarizing the key points verbally and deferring the decision.

context_blocks.header: [13] POL-028-v1.5.pdf — Office & Meeting Room Policy > 3. Meeting rooms (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Meeting rooms

Meeting rooms are available at both offices for conversations, workshops, video calls, and interviews. You can book them through Perch, just like desks. Each room shows its capacity, equipment, and location on the floor plan.

Room bookings work on a first-come, first-served basis. For recurring meetings, please be considerate: each person may hold at most 3 slots of recurring room bookings. This ensures that no single team or individual blocks a room for the whole week, and that others can find space when they need it.

If you need a room for a one-off meeting, book it as soon as you know the date. If the room you want is taken, check the floor plan for an alternative. Many rooms have similar setups, and a slightly different room often works just as well.

Please start and end your meeting on time. If you finish early, release the room in Perch so others can use it. If you are running late and someone else is waiting, they may knock and ask about the remaining time — please be gracious.

Video calls from a meeting room: check that the camera and microphone work before you start. If you are the remote participant, be aware that the room may have several people. Use the room display to see everyone clearly.

Meeting rooms are not storage spaces. Please remove your materials, notes, and personal items when your meeting ends. If you notice a room is left untidy, you can report it through Perch or to Workplace & Operations.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer who works with clients in Poland, visits the Berlin office for a workshop. He books a room for the afternoon through Perch. His team also has a weekly sync that recurs, but he holds only one recurring booking, so he is well within the limit.

If you need a room outside normal office hours, please check with Workplace & Operations first. Some rooms may be available, but we need to ensure the building is accessible and that cleaning schedules are respected.

Doc Id: POL-020-DE · Version: 1.1 · Effective Date: 2025-09-01 · Owner: Leadership Team · Classification: internal

Meeting Culture Guideline

1. Zweck

Besprechungen sind ein Mittel zum Zweck: Sie helfen uns, uns abzustimmen, Entscheidungen zu treffen und die Arbeit voranzubringen. Sie sind nicht die Arbeit selbst. Diese Richtlinie beschreibt, wie wir bei der Kranich Software GmbH Besprechungen planen, durchführen und daran teilnehmen, damit die Zeit aller respektiert wird – unabhängig davon, wo sie arbeiten oder zu welchem Team sie gehören.

Diese Version ersetzt Version 1.0 der POL-020. Sie spiegelt wider, was wir gelernt haben, seit das Unternehmen über ein einzelnes Büro hinausgewachsen und remote-first in Deutschland, Portugal, Spanien, Polen, Frankreich und dem Vereinigten Königreich geworden ist. Das Leadership Team ist für diese Richtlinie verantwortlich, und wir überprüfen sie immer dann, wenn sich unsere Arbeitsweisen wesentlich ändern.

Wir haben diese Richtlinie für alle bei Kranich geschrieben – für Ingenieur:innen, Produktmanager:innen, Customer Success Manager:innen, Field Solutions Engineers und Menschen in unterstützenden Funktionen. Sie gilt für interne Besprechungen und für Besprechungen mit externen Parteien, bei denen Kranich den Termin einberuft. Wenn Sie unsicher sind, ob eine Besprechung notwendig ist, verzichten Sie lieber auf die Terminplanung und kommunizieren Sie stattdessen asynchron.

5. Fragen

Wenn Sie Fragen zu dieser Richtlinie haben, wenden Sie sich zunächst an Ihre Führungskraft oder Ihre Teamleitung. Bei praktischen Fragen zu Planungstools oder Kalendereinstellungen kontaktieren Sie it-help@kranich.example. Bei Fragen dazu, wie diese Richtlinie mit anderen Richtlinien wie POL-004 zum Remote-Arbeiten zusammenspielt, wenden Sie sich an people@kranich.example, und wir verweisen Sie an die richtige Stelle.

Wenn Sie der Meinung sind, dass eine Besprechung, an der Sie teilnehmen, unnötig, verschwenderisch oder schlecht moderiert ist, sagen Sie das konstruktiv – der Moderatorin oder dem Moderator oder Ihrer Führungskraft. Wir hören lieber von einem Problem, als es fortbestehen zu lassen. Wenn Ihnen außerdem auffällt, dass eine wiederkehrende Besprechung von ihrem Zweck abgedriftet ist, schlagen Sie vor, sie abzusagen oder ihr Format zu ändern.

Das Leadership Team überprüft diese Richtlinie regelmäßig. Wir freuen uns über Verbesserungsvorschläge von allen bei Kranich, ob Sie nun im Berliner Büro, im Lissaboner Büro oder remote aus einem anderen Land arbeiten. Senden Sie Ihre Ideen an people@kranich.example, und wir berücksichtigen sie im nächsten Überprüfungszyklus.

Beispiel: Lea, eine People Operations Specialistin in Berlin, erhält eine Frage von einer neuen Kollegin, ob sie während der Fokuszeit eine Besprechung für einen dringenden Kundenanruf planen darf. Lea erklärt die Regel und bietet dann eine Alternative an: Die Kollegin kann den Kunden bitten, den Anruf zu verschieben, oder, falls das nicht möglich ist, eine Ausnahme bei ihrer Führungskraft beantragen. Die Richtlinie ist klar, aber nicht starr – wir vertrauen darauf, dass Menschen in seltenen Situationen ihr Urteilsvermögen einsetzen.

Besprechungen sind ein Werkzeug für Zusammenarbeit, kein Ersatz dafür. Indem wir Fokuszeit schützen, Entscheidungsrunden klein halten und standardmäßig asynchron arbeiten, geben wir einander den Raum, unsere beste Arbeit zu leisten. Vielen Dank, dass Sie uns helfen, Besprechungen sinnvoll zu gestalten.

Doc Id: HR-1ON1 · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2025-06-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

1:1 Meetings Guide

1. Purpose

Regular 1:1 meetings are one of the most important habits we build at Kranich Software. They give you and your manager dedicated, uninterrupted time to step back from daily tasks and talk about what matters: your work, your growth, and how you are feeling about both.

A good 1:1 is not a status update. Status updates belong in project channels or async updates. A 1:1 is a space for conversation, feedback, and support — for you to raise what is on your mind and for your manager to help you navigate challenges and opportunities.

This guide describes how we run 1:1s across the company, so that everyone has a consistent, useful experience regardless of team or location.

2. Who this is for

This guide applies to every employee at Kranich Software, in all teams and all locations — whether you work from the Ritterstraße office in Berlin, the Rua do Alecrim office in Lisbon, or remotely from home in Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France, or the United Kingdom.

It is written primarily for two audiences:

•  Employees who have a manager and want to make the most of their 1:1 time. •  Managers who run 1:1s and want a clear, shared framework.

If you are an engineering manager, a team lead, or anyone else who manages people, this guide is your reference. If you are a people manager of managers, you should also hold 1:1s with your direct reports and use the same principles.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, meets with her manager every few weeks. She uses the time to talk about a difficult client relationship and to ask for coaching on how to handle the next conversation. Her manager listens, asks questions, and shares a relevant approach from another team. Deniz leaves with a clearer plan.

3. Process

context_blocks.header: [18] POL-020-DE.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 3. Gute Besprechungen durchführen (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text: 3. Gute Besprechungen durchführen Jede Besprechung sollte einen klaren Zweck und eine benannte Moderatorin oder einen benannten Moderator haben. Die Moderatorin oder der Moderator ist verantwortlich für die Tagesordnung, das Tempo und das Ergebnis. Wenn einer Besprechung eine Tagesordnung fehlt, sollte die Moderatorin oder der Moderator sie absagen oder umgehend eine senden. Entscheidungsbesprechungen sind auf 6 Personen begrenzt. Diese Begrenzung hält Diskussionen fokussiert und stellt sicher, dass alle Anwesenden wirklich einen Beitrag leisten können. Wenn eine Entscheidung eine größere Gruppe betrifft, teilt die Moderatorin oder der Moderator das Ergebnis im Nachhinein mit und lädt innerhalb eines angemessenen Zeitrahmens zu Feedback ein, anstatt den Teilnehmerkreis zu erweitern. Bevor Sie eine Besprechung planen, fragen Sie sich: Was müssen wir erreichen, und wer muss wirklich im Raum sein? Laden Sie Personen ein, weil sie zum Ergebnis beitragen können, nicht weil sie möglicherweise interessiert sind. Sie können Notizen jederzeit mit Personen teilen, die nicht eingeladen sind. Für wiederkehrende Besprechungen überprüfen Sie die Teilnehmerliste und die Tagesordnung mindestens einmal pro Quartal. Streichen Sie Termine, die keinen Zweck mehr erfüllen. Es ist besser, eine wiederkehrende Besprechung früher zu beenden, als sie dahintreiben zu lassen. Beispiel: Deniz, eine Customer Success Managerin in Berlin, möchte eine Eskalation eines Kunden mit Marek, einem Field Solutions Engineer in Polen, und Sofia, einer Produktmanagerin im Fleet Insights in Spanien, besprechen. Deniz hält die Besprechung auf sich selbst und die drei anderen Personen begrenzt, weil die Entscheidung niemanden sonst erfordert. Danach veröffentlicht sie eine kurze Zusammenfassung in Grove für das gesamte Customer Success Team. Besprechungshygiene ist wichtig. Beginnen Sie pünktlich, beenden Sie pünktlich, und nehmen Sie sich am Ende ein oder zwei Minuten Zeit, um nächste Schritte und Verantwortliche zu bestätigen. Wenn Sie zu spät kommen oder früher gehen müssen, sagen Sie das zu Beginn.

context_blocks.header: [19] POL-028-v1.0.pdf — Office & Meeting Room Policy > 3. Meeting rooms (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Meeting rooms

Each office has several meeting rooms of different sizes. You can book a room through Perch, just like a desk. Rooms are bookable for internal meetings, client calls, interviews, and workshops.

Please book a room only when you truly need one. If you are meeting online and everyone is remote, a room is not necessary. If you are in the office and need a quiet space for a call, you may use a free room for a short period without booking, as long as no one has reserved it.

For recurring meetings, be mindful of how much you reserve. Each person may hold at most 3 slots of recurring room bookings. A slot is one recurring booking, such as a weekly team meeting or a monthly review. If you need more recurring slots, please contact Workplace & Operations to discuss options; we may be able to suggest a different room or an alternative pattern.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, has a weekly team sync and a biweekly planning session. She books both as recurring meetings in Perch. When she starts a new working group that also meets weekly, she realizes she would hold a third recurring slot. That is fine, but she cannot add a fourth recurring meeting without releasing one of the existing slots.

If you book a room and do not need it, cancel the booking in Perch. Rooms that are booked but unused block colleagues who need them. The same applies if your meeting ends early: please release the room for the remaining time.

Please start and end your meetings on time. If you are running late, the room may be taken by someone else after a reasonable wait, especially if it was not booked. For booked rooms, Perch will show your booking, but we ask everyone to be considerate of others' time.

Meeting rooms have video conferencing equipment. If you have trouble with the equipment, please contact it-help@kranich.example. Do not move equipment between rooms. If you use a whiteboard, please clean it after your meeting.

2. Fokuszeit

Tiefe Arbeit erfordert ununterbrochene Zeiträume. Wir schützen diese Zeit bewusst. Jeder Werktag Nachmittag umfasst 2 Stunden unternehmensweite Fokuszeit ohne Besprechungen. Während dieser Stunden können Sie jede Besprechungseinladung ohne Erklärung ablehnen, und Sie sollten nicht mit einer sofortigen Antwort auf Nachrichten rechnen.

Fokuszeit ist keine Pause. Sie ist ein gemeinsames Versprechen, einander Denkraum zu geben. Wenn Sie sich im Ritterstraße-Büro in Berlin oder im Rua do Alecrim-Büro in Lissabon befinden, behandeln Sie die Fokuszeit als ruhige Zeit in den Gemeinschaftsräumen. Wenn Sie von zu Hause arbeiten, lassen Sie Ihren Haushalt wissen, dass ein Anruf unwahrscheinlich ist.

Beispiel: Anna, eine Backend-Ingenieurin im Routing Core in Lissabon, nutzt die Fokuszeit, um eine komplexe Routing-Restriktion gründlich zu durchdenken. Sie weiß, dass ihre Kolleg:innen in Berlin in diesem Zeitfenster keinen Anruf planen werden, sodass sie die Zeit bedenkenlos als beschäftigt in ihrem Kalender blockieren kann.

Wenn Sie über das unternehmensweite Zeitfenster hinaus zusätzliche Fokuszeit benötigen, können Sie Ihren Kalender gerne als beschäftigt markieren. Die Standarderwartung ist, dass Sie außerhalb des geschützten Zeitfensters für Besprechungen verfügbar sind, aber gelegentliche Blöcke für tiefe Arbeit sind normal und gesund.

context_blocks.header: [21] POL-013-v2.0.pdf — Working Time & Overtime Policy > 2. Working time (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
2. Working time

Working time means the hours you spend performing your duties for Kranich Software GmbH. It includes time spent on internal meetings, client calls, project work, and other activities you do as part of your role. It does not include breaks, personal time, or voluntary activities outside your responsibilities.

Your regular working time is agreed in your employment contract and reflects your role, your location, and your team. Most of us work a standard full-time schedule, but part-time arrangements exist and are respected. We trust you to structure your day in a way that suits your work and your life, as long as you meet your commitments and remain available for collaboration during core hours relevant to your team.

Working time may not exceed 44 hours in any week. This is an upper limit, not a target. We expect most weeks to be shorter. If you find yourself regularly approaching this limit, please speak with your manager. It may be a sign that your workload needs adjustment.

We also encourage you to take breaks during the day. A short pause helps you stay focused and productive. Please make sure you step away from your screen regularly, especially when working remotely.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, usually works about eight hours a day. During a release week, she works a bit longer on two days. She still stays well below the weekly limit and takes a longer lunch break the following Friday.

context_blocks.header: [22] HR-REMOTEMGR.pdf — Managing Remote Teams > 3. Process > 3.2 Communicate with intention (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3.2 Communicate with intention

Do not assume silence means everything is fine. In a remote setting, you have to check in deliberately. Use the internal tools we have: Perch for booking time together, and Grove for sharing notes and decisions.

Prefer asynchronous communication by default. Write clear, concise messages that a colleague in another time zone can act on without waiting for you. When a topic is complex or

sensitive, switch to a video call.

3.3 Run meetings that respect attention

Meetings are a scarce resource in a remote company. Before scheduling one, ask whether the goal can be achieved asynchronously. When you do meet:

•  Share an agenda beforehand. •  Start and end on time. •  Give everyone a chance to speak, especially quieter team members. •  Capture decisions and action items during the call.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, leads a team with colleagues in Poland and Spain. She schedules the weekly team call during the overlap in the middle of the day, shares the agenda the day before, and rotates who facilitates the discussion.

3.4 Support wellbeing and boundaries

Remote work can blur the line between home and work. Watch for signs that a team member is overworking or feels isolated. Encourage them to take breaks and to disconnect at the end of their day.

Respect their documented working hours. If you send a message outside those hours, make clear that a response is not expected until their next working day. Never praise someone primarily for how many hours they put in; praise outcomes and quality.

context_blocks.header: [25] POL-020-v1.0.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 4. Async first (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
4. Async first

We are a remote-first company, and our default mode of work is asynchronous. Before you schedule a meeting, ask yourself whether the goal can be achieved without one. A document, a recorded demo, a shared spreadsheet, or a thoughtful message on a collaboration channel often works better than a live call — especially when participants span time zones from Lisbon to Warsaw.

When you do work asynchronously, be generous with context. Write clear subject lines, summarise decisions in a few sentences, and state explicitly when you need a response and by when. Use the tools we have — Grove for policies, Fern for people data, Ledgerly for expenses, 1Password for credentials — and remember that not everyone reads every channel every day.

If a discussion in a channel goes back and forth more than a few times, that is a signal to move it to a short synchronous conversation. Async does not mean slow; it means thoughtful. When a decision requires rapid iteration or high emotional nuance, a meeting is the right tool.

Sofia, a product manager in Fleet Insights working remotely from Spain, drafts a product decision document and shares it with her team a few days before the decision deadline. Colleagues comment asynchronously, and Sofia incorporates their feedback. By the time the team meets, the discussion is short and the decision is almost made. The meeting exists to confirm, not to discover.

context_blocks.header: [26] HR-1ON1.pdf — 1:1 Meetings Guide > 3. Process > After the meeting (p. 2–3)
context_blocks.text:
After the meeting

Follow up on what you agreed. If you said you would do something, do it promptly. If you raised a concern, check back on it in the next 1:1. This follow-through builds trust and shows that the meeting matters.

4. Timelines

1:1s should happen on a regular, ongoing basis throughout the year. There is no fixed schedule that applies to everyone — the right frequency depends on your role, your experience, and the nature of your work.

As a general expectation:

•  New employees should meet with their manager more frequently during their first weeks to support onboarding and early alignment. •  People in new or changing roles may benefit from a temporary increase in frequency until they feel settled. •  Experienced employees in stable roles may prefer a lighter cadence, but should still meet regularly enough that conversations feel continuous rather than occasional.

If you feel that your 1:1s are too rare or too frequent, say so. Your manager can adjust. If you and your manager disagree about the right cadence, escalate to your manager's manager or to People & Culture.

Additionally, at least once per year, every employee should have a dedicated conversation about their development and performance that goes beyond the regular 1:1. This conversation is separate from day-to-day check-ins and is described in the relevant People & Culture policy (see POL-004). Your manager will schedule this conversation for you.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer who works with clients in Poland, recently moved into a new account territory. His manager proposes meeting every week for the first few weeks to help him get oriented, then returning to the usual rhythm. Marek agrees, and the extra check- ins help him clarify expectations with two new clients early on.

context_blocks.header: [27] HR-1ON1.pdf — 1:1 Meetings Guide > 3. Process > Scheduling and cadence (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
Scheduling and cadence

Your manager is responsible for scheduling regular 1:1s with you. If you do not have a recurring meeting on your calendar, ask your manager to set one up, or reach out to People & Culture for help.

The cadence should be regular and predictable. Most teams meet every week or every other week. Choose a rhythm that works for both of you and stick to it. Reschedule rather than cancel whenever possible — a 1:1 that is skipped repeatedly sends a signal that the conversation is not important.

Agenda

You own the agenda. This is your time, and you should bring what you want to discuss. A few categories to consider:

•  Current work: what is going well, what is blocked, where you need input. •  Feedback: both giving and receiving. Praise, concerns, and suggestions for improvement. •  Growth and development: skills you want to build, roles you are curious about, long- term aspirations. •  Well-being and workload: how you are doing, whether the pace is sustainable, and what support you need. •  Team and company: observations, ideas, and questions about how things work around you.

Your manager may also add items to the agenda — for example, to share updates, give feedback, or align on priorities. Both sides should prepare a little before the meeting so the time is used well.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, keeps a running list of topics in her notes app. Before her 1:1, she adds two items: a question about how the Routing Core team plans its technical debt work, and a request for feedback on the code review she submitted last week. When the meeting starts, she shares her screen and walks through her list.

During the meeting

Start by checking in on how the other person is doing — genuinely. Then move through the agenda. As a manager, listen more than you speak. Ask open questions. Resist the urge to jump into problem-solving mode immediately; often the employee has a solution in mind and just needs space to articulate it.

Take notes during the meeting, but keep your attention on the conversation. After the meeting, write down any action items and who owns them.

context_blocks.header: [28] POL-013-v1.5.pdf — Working Time & Overtime Policy > 5. Questions (p. 3)
context_blocks.text:
5. Questions

If you have questions about this policy, start with your manager. They can help you apply it to your day-to-day work. For questions about time recording in Fern, contact it- help@kranich.example. For anything related to your employment contract, local rules, or how this policy interacts with other policies such as POL-004, contact People & Culture at people@kranich.example.

We want this policy to feel straightforward. If a situation is not covered here, use your judgement, talk to your manager, and err on the side of rest. Working long hours does not help you, your team, or our clients. Taking your time off and staying within the weekly limit is part of doing your job well.

context_blocks.header: [29] POL-013-v1.0.pdf — Working Time & Overtime Policy > 2. Working time (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
2. Working time

Kranich is a remote-first company. Most of us work from home within our country of employment — Germany, Portugal, Spain, Poland, France, and the United Kingdom. We also have offices in Berlin (Ritterstraße) and Lisbon (Rua do Alecrim) for those who prefer to work on-site, and we use Perch to book desks and meeting rooms when you visit.

Your working time is the time you spend performing work-related duties for Kranich. This includes your regular daily work, participation in meetings with colleagues or clients, and any other tasks that are part of your role. It does not include breaks, commuting, or voluntary activities outside of work.

We expect you to organise your working time so that you can fulfil the responsibilities of your role while maintaining a healthy balance. For most roles, this means a standard full-time schedule distributed across the working days of the week. Part-time arrangements are possible and should be discussed with your manager and recorded in Fern.

As a general rule, working time may not exceed 44 hours in any week. This limit applies to all employees, regardless of whether the work is performed during regular hours or as overtime. We set this limit to protect your health and to ensure that you have sufficient time for rest and recovery between working periods.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, sometimes needs to coordinate with colleagues in different time zones. She plans her week so that her total working time stays within the limit, even on weeks when an early-morning call with a client in Poland shifts her schedule.

If you find that your workload regularly requires you to approach the weekly limit, please speak with your manager. That is a signal that we need to redistribute work or adjust priorities, not a sign that you should simply work longer hours.

context_blocks.header: [30] POL-002-v1.0.pdf — Remote Work Policy > 3. Working hours and availability (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Working hours and availability

Remote work does not change the expectations around your working hours. We trust you to structure your day in a way that lets you do your best work while also being available for

collaboration with your team and colleagues.

As a general principle, we expect you to be reachable during the core hours that your team agrees upon. Many teams have colleagues across different time zones, from Lisbon to Warsaw, so we ask everyone to be thoughtful about scheduling meetings and to respect each other's focus time.

When you work remotely, you should:

•  Keep your calendar up to date, including your working hours and any breaks. •  Respond to messages and meeting invitations promptly during your working hours. •  Let your team know if you are unavailable for an extended period during the day. •  Join meetings with your camera on when possible, so that remote participants feel equally included.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, starts her day at eight in the morning so she can support clients in earlier time zones. She blocks an hour for lunch and finishes at four in the afternoon. Her calendar reflects these hours, and her team knows when to expect her.

We do not prescribe specific start or end times, because we know that personal circumstances differ. What matters is that you deliver on your responsibilities and that your team can rely on you. If your working pattern changes, update your calendar and let your manager know.
