7. Working hours

The standard working week in Germany is 38.0 hours per week. This is the basis for full-time employment. Your individual contract states whether you are full-time or part-time and, if part- time, your agreed weekly hours.

We are a remote-first company, and we trust you to structure your working day in a way that suits your role and your team. Within the framework of German working time law, you are responsible for taking adequate breaks and for not exceeding maximum daily working hours. Your manager is responsible for planning workloads so that you can work healthy hours.

Core collaboration times may be set by your team. If your team agrees on common hours for meetings or stand-ups, please respect them. Outside those times, you are free to organize your work as long as you meet your commitments and your contractual hours.

Overtime is not a regular expectation. If your role occasionally requires more hours, for

example during a critical release or a client go-live, your manager will discuss this with you in advance and agree on compensatory time off. Please record your working time in the tool provided by your manager, as required by German law.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, works full-time on a 38.0 hours per week basis. Her team has a daily stand-up at a time that works for colleagues in Germany and Portugal. Anna starts her day a little later, takes a proper lunch break, and finishes in the early evening. When a release requires extra evening work, her manager agrees on time off in lieu the following week.

If you consistently struggle to complete your work within your contractual hours, please speak with your manager. It is a sign that priorities or capacity need adjusting, not that you should work longer hours.

context_blocks.text:
4. Async first

Asynchrone Kommunikation ist unser Standard. Wir arbeiten über Zeitzonen hinweg von Berlin bis Lissabon und darüber hinaus, und wir gehen nicht davon aus, dass alle kurzfristig an einem Live-Anruf teilnehmen können. Schreiben Sie Dinge auf, teilen Sie sie in Grove oder im entsprechenden Kanal, und lassen Sie Menschen antworten, wenn sie dazu in der Lage sind.

Nutzen Sie eine Besprechung nur dann, wenn ein Live-Gespräch einen Mehrwert bietet: Brainstorming, das von schnellem Hin und Her profitiert, die Lösung eines Konflikts oder eine Entscheidung, die Diskussion statt einer einfachen Abstimmung erfordert. Für alles andere bevorzugen Sie Dokumente, aufgezeichnete Updates oder schriftliche Fragen.

Wenn Sie ein Dokument zur Rückmeldung teilen, geben Sie die Frist für Kommentare klar an und benennen Sie die Entscheidungsverantwortlichen. Wenn Sie eine Antwort benötigen, stellen Sie eine direkte Frage, anstatt ein Dokument zu veröffentlichen und auf Antworten zu hoffen.

Beispiel: Sofia, eine Produktmanagerin im Fleet Insights, die remote aus Spanien arbeitet, möchte Input zu einer vorgeschlagenen Änderung, wie wir Flotten-Gesundheitswerte darstellen. Statt einen Termin mit mehreren Beteiligten zu planen, schreibt sie einen kurzen

Vorschlag, veröffentlicht ihn im Fleet-Insights-Kanal und bittet um Kommentare bis zum Ende der Woche. Kolleg:innen in Polen und im Vereinigten Königreich antworten asynchron, und Sofia arbeitet ihr Feedback ein, bevor der nächste Team-Sync stattfindet.

Wenn Sie eine Besprechung planen, teilen Sie die Tagesordnung und etwaiges Vorabmaterial mindestens einen Tag im Voraus. Nutzen Sie die Besprechungszeit nicht für stilles Lesen. Wenn Teilnehmende das Material nicht lesen konnten, erwägen Sie, den Termin zu verschieben oder die Kernpunkte mündlich zusammenzufassen und die Entscheidung aufzuschieben.

answer_text:
The latest update in the supplied context is [33] (MTG-06, effective 2025-07-19), which states: **“The deploy window is 7 hours per day. This applies to all production changes to the Routing Core and Fleet Insights services, effective immediately.”** [33]

context_blocks.text: 4. Patching Keeping software up to date is one of the most effective ways to protect against known vulnerabilities. This standard sets clear expectations for how quickly patches must be applied, and it applies to the operating system, browsers, productivity software, development tools, and any other software installed on company-managed devices. Critical patches are installed within 12 calendar days of release. This applies to patches that address vulnerabilities with a known exploit or that are rated critical by the software vendor. Our device management tool tracks patch status centrally, and it-help monitors compliance. If a critical patch cannot be applied within the required window — for example, because of a compatibility issue with a specialized tool — you must notify it-help promptly so they can track the exception and apply a compensating control. For non-critical patches, including routine operating system updates and feature releases, we expect them to be installed as soon as they are available, and no later than the next scheduled maintenance window. Automatic updates should remain enabled at all times. If you see a prompt to restart your device to complete an update, do not postpone it indefinitely — a restart takes only a few minutes and closes the window of exposure. Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, receives a notification that a critical security patch is available for her laptop's operating system. She is in the middle of a customer call, so she dismisses the reminder and continues working. Later that day, she sees a second reminder from the device management tool and restarts her laptop during her lunch break. The patch is installed well within the 12 calendar days window, and Deniz has not put any customer data at risk. Software that is no longer supported by its vendor — sometimes called end-of-life software — must not be installed on company devices. Unsupported software does not receive patches, which means it can never meet the requirements of this standard. If you need a piece of software that is no longer supported, discuss alternatives with your manager and it-help. In rare cases, an exception may be granted for a specific business need, but the exception must be documented and must include compensating controls. Patching applies to all devices, regardless of where you work.

2. Cadence

We publish release notes on a regular schedule that aligns with our product delivery cycles. Customers can expect an update whenever a meaningful change ships, rather than waiting for a fixed calendar date.

Release notes appear in the Grove customer portal and are also distributed by email to the customer contacts we have on file. Customer Success may share highlights in account reviews, but the release notes themselves remain the authoritative record.

Each set of release notes follows a consistent structure:

•  Summary – one or two sentences describing the change in plain language. •  What changed – a short description of the behavior before and after the update. •  Why it matters – the benefit to the customer’s daily operation. •  Action required – only included when the customer must do something, such as updating an integration or confirming a new setting.

We group changes by module. When a change spans more than one module, we note it in each relevant section and link to the primary entry.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, works with a customer who asks whether a routing improvement affects their nightly batch. Deniz checks the latest release notes and sees the change listed under Routing Core with a note that no action is required. She forwards the entry to the customer, who can plan accordingly.

We aim to publish release notes promptly after a change is available to customers. If a change is rolled out gradually, we publish the notes when the first customers receive it and add a note that availability may vary.

Occasionally we publish an emergency fix that affects only a subset of customers. In that case, we still write release notes, but we may keep them brief and notify affected customers directly through Customer Success.

4. Rollback

Every release must have a rollback plan. The rollback plan is part of the release notes and is reviewed by the release coordinator before deployment begins.

Rollback means returning the production environment to the previous known-good state. For most releases, this is done by redeploying the previous artifact. For releases that include database migrations, the rollback plan must state explicitly whether the migration is reversible and what the reversal steps are.

If a release causes a customer-facing incident, the default decision is to roll back first and investigate later. Speed matters. Do not spend time trying to fix forward if a rollback restores service promptly.

The rollback decision is made by the release coordinator, in consultation with the on-call engineer and the engineering manager of the affected team. If the incident involves a major customer, the release coordinator informs the Head of Workplace & Operations, Rui Almeida, who coordinates with Customer Success.

After a rollback, the team holds a brief review to understand what happened and what should change before the next attempt. The review is blameless. We are looking for process improvements, not individuals at fault.

Example: Sofia, a product manager in Fleet Insights, ships a new reporting view. Shortly after deployment, Customer Success reports that a customer sees incorrect totals. The release coordinator decides to roll back. The previous version is restored within minutes. The team later finds that the issue was a data transformation error, fixes it, and ships the view again in the next release.

5. Questions

If you have questions about the release process, start by asking in the engineering channel or your team channel. The release coordinator for the current week is the best first point of contact.

For questions about a specific release, including freeze windows and rollback plans, contact the release coordinator directly. For broader process feedback, reach out to the Head of Information Security, Priya Nayar, or the CTO, Jonas Weber.

If you notice that this guide is out of date, suggest an update through Grove. The owner of this document is Platform & Infrastructure, and they review it regularly alongside related policies

such as POL-004.

For questions about how releases interact with customer contracts or rate changes, refer to FIN-RATES-2026 and speak with your manager or the finance team.

Doc Id: ENG-GUIDE-RELEASE · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2025-05-01 · Owner: Platform & Infrastructure · Classification: internal

Release Process

1. Purpose

This guide describes how Kranich Route Cloud releases are planned, executed, and, if needed, undone. It is written for engineers, product managers, and customer-facing teams who need to know what happens when code ships.

A release is more than merging to main. It is a coordinated event that involves Routing Core, Fleet Insights, Platform & Infrastructure, and Customer Success. This guide sets expectations so everyone can work together calmly and predictably.

We aim for releases that are boring. If a release is boring, it means the preparation was thorough, the rollout was smooth, and customers noticed nothing except improvements.

2. Cadence

Kranich Route Cloud follows a regular release cadence. Platform & Infrastructure owns the schedule and communicates it through the engineering calendar and Grove.

Most releases are incremental and small. We prefer shipping frequently over batching many changes into one large release. Small releases are easier to review, easier to test, and easier to roll back if something goes wrong.

Each release goes through the same stages:

•  Code review and automated checks •  Staging deployment and verification •  Production deployment, phased by customer cohort •  Post-release monitoring

The release coordinator for the week is named in the team channel. That person is the single point of contact for release-related questions and decisions. If you are unsure whether your change belongs in an upcoming release, ask the release coordinator.

Feature flags are the default mechanism for controlling exposure. If a feature is not ready for all customers, it ships behind a flag. This keeps the release cadence steady even when individual features are still maturing.

Doc Id: ENG-ADR-04 · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2025-05-20 · Owner: Platform & Infrastructure · Classification: internal

ADR-04: Pipeline time budget

1. Status

Accepted.

2. Context

The Platform & Infrastructure team maintains the continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines that build, test, and deploy the Kranich Route Cloud. Over the past year, pipeline runtime has grown noticeably as the codebase expanded and the test suite matured. Several teams reported that waiting for a full pipeline run slowed down their work, particularly when a change touched multiple services at once.

We evaluated what we wanted the pipeline to guarantee. A clear upper bound helps engineers plan their day and reduces the temptation to bypass checks for the sake of speed. It also gives the Platform & Infrastructure team a concrete target when optimizing build steps, caching, and parallelization.

We considered a few options. One was to leave the pipeline unconstrained and rely on teams to optimize their own steps; this had led to the current drift. Another was to set a strict budget that applied to every commit, including trivial documentation changes; that felt unnecessarily rigid. A third option, which we chose, was to define a single budget for the full pipeline and to treat it as a hard ceiling, while allowing teams to propose exceptions through the normal change process.

The decision aligns with the engineering principles we already follow, including the guidance on deployment practices in POL-004. It also complements the financial guardrails described in FIN-RATES-2026, which govern how we allocate infrastructure spend; a time budget indirectly protects that spend by discouraging wasteful pipeline configurations.

3. Maintenance

We perform maintenance on the Kranich Route Cloud to keep it secure, reliable, and up to date. We distinguish between two types of maintenance: scheduled and emergency.

Scheduled maintenance is planned in advance and announced to customers through the status page and by email. We schedule this work for periods of typically lower usage, and we aim to keep each window short. We will notify you at least a few days before the maintenance begins, with a clear description of what we are doing and the expected impact.

Emergency maintenance is required to address a security vulnerability, a service disruption, or another issue that cannot wait for the next scheduled window. In these cases we will notify you as promptly as possible, even if the notice period is short. We will keep you informed as the work progresses.

Maintenance windows do not count against the monthly uptime commitment described in §2. However, we will make every effort to minimize the frequency and duration of maintenance so that your operations are affected as little as possible.

context_blocks.header: [13] ENG-TEAM-03.pdf — Team Charter — Platform & Infrastructure > 3. How we work (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. How we work

We work in two-week iterations and plan in six-week cycles. At the start of each cycle, the whole team gathers for a planning session where squads present their proposed commitments. We deliberately leave slack in every cycle for unplanned operational work and small improvements that never make it onto a roadmap.

All code changes go through peer review. We require a second pair of eyes on every pull request, and changes to production infrastructure need approval from the owning squad's tech lead. We practice blameless post-incident reviews: the goal is to learn what broke in our processes, not who broke them.

We hold a weekly demo where any team member can show what they built, even if it is unfinished. We hold a weekly retro where we discuss what went well and what we want to change. Both meetings are optional, and recordings are available for those in different time zones. We default to asynchronous communication on our team channel and reserve

synchronous time for problems that benefit from live discussion.

Documentation is part of done. A change is not complete until the relevant runbooks, architecture diagrams, and onboarding guides are updated. If a document is not useful, we delete it rather than let it rot.

context_blocks.header: [14] ENG-RFC-09.pdf — RFC-09: Background job scheduler > 4. Alternatives considered > 4.4 External task runner (p. 3–4)
context_blocks.text:
4.4 External task runner

We briefly considered triggering jobs through an external task runner invoked by cron. This works for periodic work but is a poor fit for event-driven jobs such as "recalculate after this import finishes". The scheduler supports both patterns: periodic jobs are enqueued by a lightweight cron loop inside the scheduler, while event-driven jobs are enqueued via the API.

5. Rollout

Platform & Infrastructure will build the scheduler in the current quarter. We will start with a small set of internal jobs that we own, to validate the operational model.

In the following quarter, we will invite Routing Core and Fleet Insights to migrate their first job types. The migration for each job type follows the same pattern: move the handler code into the scheduler deployment, enqueue from the service instead of executing inline, and verify behaviour in staging.

Customer Success will not need to change anything immediately. Their ad-hoc scripts will continue to work, but we will offer a path to move recurring webhook retries onto the scheduler

once the service is stable.

During the transition, both the old inline execution path and the new scheduler path will exist. Teams can switch a job type back if they encounter issues. We expect the old paths to be removed by the end of the year.

6. Open questions

•  Should the scheduler support priority classes for jobs, or is a single FIFO-with-delay queue sufficient for our current needs? •  Do we need per-tenant isolation for job queues, given that Kranich Route Cloud serves multiple logistics operators from the same deployment? •  How should we handle jobs whose payload references data that has been deleted by the time the job runs? Should the scheduler enforce a maximum job age? •  What is the right owner for the dead-letter review process? Platform & Infrastructure can build the tooling, but each team should probably review its own dead jobs. •  Should periodic jobs be defined declaratively in configuration, or remain code-level constructs inside the scheduler?

context_blocks.header: [16] ENG-ADR-06.pdf — ADR-06: Migration lock timeouts > 4. Consequences (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
4. Consequences

The main benefit is predictability. No deployment will hold the lock indefinitely, and engineers no longer need to guess whether a stuck deployment will resolve itself. The alert gives the on- call engineer enough information to decide whether to intervene or to let the deployment pipeline retry.

The trade-off is that a legitimate migration which genuinely needs more than the timeout will fail. We accept this because a migration that runs for that long is usually a sign that it should be split into smaller steps or run as a background job outside the deployment path. Teams that hit the timeout should review the migration plan and consider batching the work.

Another consequence is that the deployment pipeline must handle the timeout abort gracefully. The pipeline already treats a failed migration as a stop condition, so no further steps run. We will update the runbook to describe the timeout behavior and the recommended follow-up.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, writes a migration that adds an index to a large table. The migration runs longer than expected because the table is heavily used. The runner aborts the migration after the timeout, and Anna receives the alert. She checks the deployment log, sees the timeout status, and rewrites the migration to build the index in batches. The next deployment succeeds.

The related policy for deployment practices is POL-004, and the cost implications for infrastructure changes are tracked under FIN-RATES-2026. No changes to those documents are required by this decision.

context_blocks.header: [17] POL-013-v1.5.pdf — Working Time & Overtime Policy > 2. Working time (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
2. Working time

Working time is the time you spend performing your duties for Kranich. It includes your regular work, client calls, internal meetings, and time spent on business travel during what would otherwise be your working hours. It does not include your lunch break, other unpaid breaks, or your commute between home and the office.

Our standard working week runs from Monday to Friday. We do not prescribe fixed start and end times; you and your manager agree on a schedule that fits your team's collaboration needs and your personal circumstances. What matters is that you are available for the meetings and tasks your role requires, and that you coordinate with colleagues across time zones.

Working time may not exceed 44 hours in any week. This limit includes overtime. We count a week from Monday to Sunday. If you work in a jurisdiction with a stricter weekly limit, the stricter limit applies to you.

We expect you to take breaks during the day. A break of at least thirty minutes is recommended when you work more than six hours. You should also take time away from the screen regularly; short walks or stretching count as breaks only if they are not part of your duties.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, usually starts at nine and finishes around five- thirty. On a week with a late deployment, she works until seven on two evenings. She keeps an eye on her total so that she stays under the weekly limit.

If you regularly need more than the standard hours to complete your work, speak with your manager. That is usually a sign that priorities need adjusting or that the team needs more support, not that you should work longer. We do not expect anyone to answer messages outside their agreed working hours, unless they are on call or have explicitly agreed otherwise

with their team.

context_blocks.header: [18] ENG-ADR-04.pdf — ADR-04: Pipeline time budget > 3. Decision (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Decision

The full pipeline must finish within 68 minutes. This budget covers the complete run from the moment a commit is picked up to the moment artifacts are ready for deployment. It includes compilation, unit and integration tests, container builds, and the packaging steps.

We define "full pipeline" as the end-to-end sequence that runs for a merge to the main branch. Short-lived checks, such as a quick lint on a pull request, are not part of this budget. However, any step that runs in the main-branch pipeline counts toward the 68 minutes, regardless of which team owns the step.

To make the budget enforceable, we add a monitoring alert that fires when a pipeline run approaches the ceiling. If a run exceeds the budget, the pipeline fails and the owning team receives a notification. The team can then investigate and either optimize the step or open a request to exempt that particular pipeline from the budget. Exemptions are reviewed by Platform & Infrastructure and are meant to be temporary; we expect teams to treat an

exemption as a prompt to refactor rather than as a permanent allowance.

We also commit to reviewing the budget on a regular cadence. If the product roadmap introduces work that fundamentally changes the build shape, we may revisit this decision, but any change to the 68 minutes will go through the same architecture review process as this document.

The team has addressed several edge cases reported by customers in recent months, and the remaining work is mostly around regression testing. - Sofia shared the Fleet Insights roadmap. The team is preparing a new dashboard view that helps dispatchers compare planned versus actual routes. She asked for input from Customer Success on how to frame the feature in user-facing messaging.
- Deniz reported that customers are generally positive about recent improvements, but some have asked for clearer communication when a planned route changes mid-day. This sparked a discussion about notification preferences and whether the platform should let customers choose the channel.

- No figures, dates beyond the current year, or numeric targets were discussed. The group will rely on qualitative milestones and the existing tracking documents.

3. Decision

We will introduce automated staging snapshots. Whenever a staging environment is torn down, Platform & Infrastructure will capture a snapshot of its data and configuration before deletion. Snapshots are stored in a dedicated, access-controlled repository, separate from production backups.

Staging snapshots are kept for 206 days. After that period, they are purged automatically by the retention job. The retention job runs regularly and is monitored by Platform & Infrastructure.

A snapshot can be restored to a fresh staging environment on request. Any engineer or customer success manager may request a restore through the internal ticketing flow; Platform & Infrastructure will perform the restore promptly, typically within the same working day. Each restored environment is clearly labelled with the snapshot id and the original creation date, so that teams know exactly what state they are working with.

Snapshots are taken only for environments that have been deliberately prepared for reuse, such as those used for integration testing or client demonstrations. Ad-hoc scratch environments are exempt, unless the person who created them explicitly marks them for snapshotting.

Access to the snapshot repository follows the same role-based rules already documented in POL-004. Audit logs record who created, restored, or deleted a snapshot.

3. Freeze windows

A release freeze starts 2 days before a major customer go-live. The freeze applies to all production changes, including configuration changes and database migrations, unless the change is explicitly approved as an exception by Platform & Infrastructure.

The purpose of a freeze is stability. When a major customer goes live, the last thing we want is an unrelated deployment introducing risk. The freeze gives the customer team and the engineering teams a quiet window to focus.

During a freeze, you may still merge code to main, but you must not deploy it to production.

You may also run read-only operations and prepare changes that are scheduled to go out after the freeze lifts.

The freeze lifts once the go-live is verified and the release coordinator announces the end of the freeze in the team channel. If the go-live is delayed, the freeze extends automatically until the new go-live date is confirmed.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, coordinates a go-live for a logistics operator in Poland. She confirms the go-live date with Marek, the field solutions engineer. Platform & Infrastructure announces the freeze. Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, has a performance improvement ready, but she waits until the freeze lifts before deploying it.

context_blocks.header: [22] POL-020-v1.0.pdf — Meeting Culture Guideline > 2. Focus time (p. 1)

2. Focus time

Deep work is the foundation of our craft. Writing code, analysing data, designing a solution, or preparing a customer workshop all require stretches of uninterrupted concentration. Constant context switching fragments our thinking and lowers the quality of everything we do.

To protect this, every weekday afternoon holds 2 hours of company-wide focus time with no meetings. During this window, you will not receive meeting invitations, and we ask you not to schedule any. This applies to all teams and all locations, including customer-facing roles. If a customer requests a meeting during focus time, offer an alternative slot the same day or the next working day; in urgent situations, speak with your manager first.

Focus time is not a break — it is working time, and you are still expected to be reachable for urgent matters through your usual channels. If something genuinely cannot wait, send a direct message rather than scheduling a meeting. We trust you to use your judgment about what counts as urgent.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, uses focus time to work through a complex routing algorithm. Her colleague in Berlin knows not to invite her to a sync during that window and instead leaves a thoughtful comment on the pull request. Anna picks it up when her focus block ends.

context_blocks.header: [23] ENG-RFC-10.pdf — RFC-10: Search over fleet documents > 5. Rollout (p. 3)
context_blocks.text:
5. Rollout

We roll out in stages, starting internally.

First, we enable Fleet Search for employees only. Customer success managers and field solutions engineers get access to the search box and see document results. We collect feedback on result quality and query behavior for a few weeks.

Second, we enable search for a small set of pilot customers. These customers already use the document upload feature heavily. We work with their success managers to confirm that access control behaves correctly and that results are useful.

Third, we enable search for all customers who have the document feature enabled. This happens after the pilot shows no access-control issues and after we have updated the user documentation in Grove.

Throughout rollout, the Platform & Infrastructure team monitors index lag and query latency. The Customer Success team owns communication with pilot customers. The Go-to-Market team prepares release notes for the general availability announcement.

Rollback is straightforward: we disable the search endpoint in the web application. The document store is unaffected, and existing upload and retrieval flows continue to work as before. The index can remain in place for a later re-enable, or it can be deleted; it is derived data and carries no state that cannot be rebuilt.

context_blocks.header: [25] ENG-ADR-06.pdf — ADR-06: Migration lock timeouts > 3. Decision (p. 1)
context_blocks.text:
3. Decision

We introduce a fixed global timeout for the advisory lock. Migrations abort after holding a lock for 94 minutes. The runner checks the elapsed time at regular intervals while the migration is in progress. When the timeout is reached, the runner aborts the migration, releases the lock, and marks the deployment as failed with a clear error message.

The timeout applies to every migration in every environment, including staging and production. It cannot be overridden by a migration script or by a deployment configuration. This keeps the behavior predictable and removes the temptation to set a per-migration exception that would undermine the guarantee.

The runner distinguishes between three outcomes: success, failure before the timeout, and timeout abort. Each outcome writes a distinct status to the deployment log. The timeout abort also triggers an alert to the Platform & Infrastructure on-call channel, so a human can investigate promptly without being paged in the middle of the night for a routine case.

4. Merging

A pull request merges when it has approval, the tests pass, and there are no unresolved must- fix comments. The author merges their own change after the reviewer approves. Do not merge your own work without a review, even for a small fix.

Before merging, rebase or merge the latest main branch. Squash commits if the history is noisy. Write a merge message that summarizes the change and references the issue. If the change affects the API or the data model, update the relevant internal documentation in the same pull request.

If a review raises a must-fix comment, address it and ask for another look. If you disagree with a comment, say so and explain your reasoning. The reviewer does not have to win; the best argument does. When you cannot agree, involve the engineering manager or the tech lead for the area.

After merging, watch the deployment. If something breaks, revert promptly rather than patching forward. A clean revert is easier for everyone to understand.

Example: Ines Duarte, an engineering manager in Berlin, reviews a routing change from Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon. Ines suggests a simpler loop. Anna explains why the loop is the way it is, and Ines agrees. They merge the change the same day.

5. Questions

If you are unsure about any part of this guide, ask your engineering manager or the Platform & Infrastructure team. For questions about security-sensitive changes, involve the Head of Information Security, Priya Nayar. For questions about how reviews fit with our incident response or release process, refer to the relevant policy documents, such as POL-004 for security handling and FIN-RATES-2026 for rate-related changes in billing.

If the process gets in the way — if a review takes too long, if the size rule feels wrong for your case, or if you want to propose a change to this guide — raise it in the engineering weekly. This guide belongs to all of us, and we update it when the practice changes.

Doc Id: ENG-ADR-03

Version: 1.0

Effective Date: 2025-04-20

Owner: Platform & Infrastructure

Classification: internal

ADR-03: Staging snapshots

1. Status

Accepted.

2. Context

The Platform & Infrastructure team maintains staging environments for Kranich Route Cloud. These environments are used by engineering teams for integration testing, by Customer Success for demonstration scenarios, and by field solutions engineers like Marek when preparing proof-of-concept sessions with prospects in Poland.

Historically, staging environments were rebuilt on demand, and the state of a staging environment was tied to whichever engineer had last modified it. This caused friction: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, might spend part of a day setting up a particular dataset for a routing test, only to find the environment reset by a colleague in Berlin the next morning. Conversely, Deniz in Customer Success once prepared a client-facing walkthrough on a staging environment that had drifted so far from production that the demonstration failed mid-session.

The team also struggled with debugging. When a defect was reported against a staging environment, the engineer investigating it had no reliable way to know what data or configuration had been present when the issue occurred. Reproducing the problem often required recreating state from memory or from scattered notes in chat threads.

We considered treating staging as fully ephemeral, with every environment destroyed after each use. That approach would have simplified storage but made cross-team collaboration harder, because a useful dataset prepared by one person could not be reused by another. We also considered keeping every staging environment indefinitely, which would have consumed excessive storage and made compliance checks cumbersome.

We need a middle ground: a consistent, auditable way to preserve staging state for a defined period, long enough for debugging and reuse, but short enough to keep storage predictable.

context_blocks.header: [32] ENG-RFC-03.docx — RFC-03: Telemetry pipeline > 4. Alternatives considered
context_blocks.text:
4. Alternatives considered

Direct database writes. Each service writes telemetry directly to a shared analytics database. This was rejected because it couples services to a particular storage technology and makes schema evolution difficult. It also places load on the database that scales with application traffic.

A third-party SaaS telemetry product. We evaluated using an external vendor for the entire pipeline. This was rejected for cost predictability and data-residency reasons, as some customer data must remain within the EU. A managed endpoint from a vendor could still be considered later for specific delivery targets, but not as the core pipeline.

Per-team pipelines. Each team continues to operate its own ingestion and storage. This was rejected because it duplicates operational burden and makes cross-team correlation hard. The whole point of a shared pipeline is to enable queries that span services, such as correlating a routing failure with a fleet data outage.

A push model from services to consumers. Services call consumer endpoints directly. This was rejected because it couples producers to consumers and makes adding new consumers a coordinated effort. The topic-based model decouples producers from consumers.

5. Rollout

The rollout happens in phases, coordinated by Platform & Infrastructure.

In the first phase, we build the pipeline in the staging environment and onboard the Routing Core services that emit the highest-volume events. We validate schema handling, retention behavior, and consumer replay.

In the second phase, we move the pipeline to production and migrate all Routing Core and Fleet Insights services. During this phase, the old per-service ingestion paths remain available but are marked deprecated.

In the third phase, we deprecate the old paths and require all new telemetry to go through the pipeline. Customer Success and Go-to-Market integrations are onboarded here.

Throughout the rollout, Platform & Infrastructure publishes a migration guide and offers office hours for teams that need help adapting their code. The rollout is complete when no service publishes telemetry outside the pipeline.

context_blocks.header: [36] ENG-RFC-02.pdf — RFC-02: Route planning latency budget > 3. Details (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Details

The p95 of 370 ms becomes the single source of truth for performance conversations about the route-planning endpoint. Teams should use this number when deciding whether an optimization is worth the complexity it introduces.

We ask each team that touches the request path to consider their contribution to the latency budget. For example, Platform & Infrastructure should keep an eye on gateway overhead and

connection pooling. Routing Core should profile solver warm-up and cache hit rates. Fleet Insights should check that any data enrichment called during planning is cached appropriately.

To make the target actionable, we will add a performance regression test to the CI pipeline. The test replays a corpus of recorded production requests against a staging environment. If the p95 of the replayed traffic exceeds the budget, the pipeline fails. The corpus is refreshed quarterly from anonymized production traces.

We also recommend that teams instrument their services with tracing spans that carry the parent request id. This makes it straightforward to find where time is spent when the endpoint misses the budget. We will publish a short runbook on how to read the traces and how to correlate them with gateway logs.

The budget applies to the default tenant configuration. We know that some customers run with unusually large fleets or complex constraints. We will work with Customer Success on a case- by-case basis for those customers, but the default product experience must meet the target.

context_blocks.header: [38] ENG-ADR-05.pdf — ADR-05: Feature flag hygiene > 3. Decision (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Decision

We adopt a time-based hygiene rule for all feature flags in the Kranich Route Cloud codebase. Stale feature flags are removed after 254 days. The clock starts on the day the flag is first introduced in a merged pull request. After that period, the flag must be removed from the codebase unless it has been explicitly re-approved by the owning team's engineering manager.

To make the rule work in practice, we add the flag creation date as a comment in the flag definition and we record the flag in the team's engineering backlog with a cleanup reminder. The owning team is responsible for scheduling the removal. If a flag still needs to exist beyond

the limit, the engineering manager writes a short justification in the backlog item and sets a new review date. This re-approval is not automatic; it requires a human decision.

We do not apply the rule to flags that guard a permanently configurable behavior, such as a customer-specific integration toggle that is meant to stay. Those flags are documented as "permanent" in the code comment and are exempt from the removal deadline. Permanent flags are reviewed annually by the owning team to confirm they are still needed.

The rule applies to all environments, including development and staging. We intentionally do not distinguish between flag types, because the complexity of maintaining different lifetimes for different flag categories outweighed the benefit.

3. Customers

Deniz gave an update from Customer Success. The team has been working closely with several customers who are preparing for seasonal peaks. The conversations have been productive, and customers appreciate the proactive advice they are receiving. Deniz encouraged everyone to keep sharing customer feedback in the relevant channels — small observations often lead to meaningful improvements.

She stressed that these are early ideas and that customer input will shape what eventually gets built. Jonas added that Platform & Infrastructure continues to invest in reliability and security. 3. Equipment budget

For each new role, Workplace & Operations sets an equipment budget. The equipment budget for a standard role is €2,000. This amount covers the laptop, monitor, and other core items listed in the standard setup. It is intended to be sufficient for a high-quality, reliable setup without requiring you to make a personal contribution.

If your role has specific needs that exceed the standard budget — for example, a field solutions engineer like Marek who needs a rugged device for client sites — your manager can request an exception. The request is reviewed by Workplace & Operations together with the relevant team lead. We ask that you discuss any special needs early in the onboarding process so that the order is not delayed.

that would improve your work but is not on the list, please share it — we are always open to suggestions.

4. Refresh cycle

We keep our equipment current so that you can work efficiently and securely. Equipment is refreshed every 36 months. When your equipment reaches this age, Workplace & Operations will contact you to arrange a replacement.

If your equipment is still working well at the refresh point, you may keep it for a little longer. If your equipment fails before the refresh point and cannot be repaired, we will replace it earlier — see §6 for details. If you change roles within the company and your new role requires different equipment, we will adjust your setup at that time rather than waiting for the regular refresh.

question: The Access Control & Identity Policy states the equipment return timeline is in another document. How many business days after my last day do I have to send back the device?
expected_answer: Equipment must be returned within 10 business days after the last working day.
answer_text:
**10 business days** after your last working day.

- POL-006 (Equipment & Hardware Policy) §5 states equipment must be returned within 10 business days after the last working day [1][2]; the German version of the same provision says "innerhalb von 10 Werktage nach dem letzten Arbeitstag" [5].
- The Offboarding Checklist cross-references this deadline: "The return deadline is set out in POL-006 §5" [17].

Not supported by the supplied context: no block of the Access Control & Identity Policy (POL-023) mentions an equipment return timeline or points to one — POL-023 v1.0 §5 and v2.0 §5 cover questions about access only [19][35]. The cross-reference to §5 of POL-006 appears in the Offboarding Checklist, not in POL-023 [17].

Doc Id: POL-006-v2.2 · Version: 2.2 · Effective Date: 2025-05-01 · Supersedes: POL-006 v1.0 · Owner: Workplace & Operations · Classification: internal

Equipment & Hardware Policy

1. Purpose

This policy explains how Kranich Software provides equipment to its employees, how equipment is refreshed, and what happens when you leave the company or when hardware is lost or damaged. We want everyone to have the tools they need to do their best work, whether they sit in the Ritterstraße office, the Rua do Alecrim office, or work remotely from home.

This version supersedes version 1.0. The main changes clarify the refresh cycle, the returning process, and how losses are handled. If you have questions after reading this policy, please reach out to Workplace & Operations or your manager.

2. Standard setup

When you join Kranich, Workplace & Operations arranges your standard setup. The setup includes a laptop, a monitor, a keyboard, a mouse, a headset, and a docking station where needed. We also provide a mobile phone for roles where client contact or on-call duties make one necessary.

Your manager chooses the role category for your position before we order equipment. The two categories are Standard role and Engineering role. Engineering roles receive a more powerful laptop because of the development and testing workloads involved. If your role changes, your manager can request a different category, and we will adjust your equipment at the next refresh cycle.

All equipment remains the property of Kranich Software. You are responsible for the care of the devices assigned to you. Please keep them in a safe place, install updates promptly, and report any technical issue to it-help@kranich.example.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, received a Standard setup when she joined. Her laptop, monitor, and headset allow her to run client calls and demos without problems. When she moved to a role that required more processing power, her manager requested an upgrade, and Deniz received new hardware at the next refresh.

4. Timelines

Timing depends on the type of departure and on local notice periods. The following principles apply:

•  Resignation with notice. The process starts as soon as People & Culture is informed. Most steps are completed before the final working day. Access to systems that are not needed for the handover is revoked promptly — do not wait until the last day. •  Mutual agreement. The same process applies, with the timeline agreed between the manager, People & Culture, and the employee. •  Departure for cause. Access is revoked immediately, in line with POL-023 §4. This decision is manager-only. Other steps follow as quickly as possible, with the employee’s dignity kept in mind. •  End of contract. For fixed-term contracts, People & Culture initiates the process a few weeks before the end date, so that the handover is not rushed.

Whatever the timeline, the handover document should be finalised a few days before the final working day, so that receiving colleagues have time to ask questions.

3. Retention

Backups are retained for 105 days. This retention period applies to all backups taken under this standard, from the moment the backup is created. After the retention period ends, the backup is deleted automatically. We do not keep backups longer than the retention period unless a legal hold requires us to do so, in which case the Information Security team coordinates with the relevant teams.

The retention period balances two needs. On the one hand, we want to be able to recover data from a few weeks or a few months ago, for example if a bug corrupts data slowly over time and we only notice later. On the other hand, keeping backups forever increases cost and creates a larger attack surface: an attacker who compromises our backup storage would have access to a long history of data. A retention period of 105 days gives us a reasonable window for recovery without holding data indefinitely.

We take a new backup on a regular basis. The exact frequency depends on the system and is defined by the Platform & Infrastructure team in the system design documents. Some systems are backed up several times a day, others once a day. The retention period applies to every backup, so we always have a rolling window of the last 105 days.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, accidentally deletes a customer's configuration while testing a new workflow. The customer notices two weeks later. Because the backup retention period is 105 days, the Platform & Infrastructure team can restore the configuration from a backup taken before the deletion. If the deletion had happened several months ago, the backup would no longer exist, and Deniz would need to recreate the configuration from other sources.

Backup deletion is automated. We do not rely on someone remembering to delete old backups. The backup system marks each backup with its creation date and deletes it once the retention period has passed. If a backup cannot be deleted because of a technical issue, the Platform & Infrastructure team investigates promptly.

Equipment & Hardware Policy

1. Zweck

Diese Richtlinie erklärt, wie Kranich Software seinen Mitarbeitenden Equipment zur Verfügung stellt, wie Equipment erneuert wird und was passiert, wenn Sie das Unternehmen verlassen oder wenn Hardware verloren geht oder beschädigt wird. Wir möchten, dass alle die Werkzeuge haben, die sie für ihre beste Arbeit benötigen – ob im Ritterstraße-Büro, im Rua-do- Alecrim-Büro oder remote von zu Hause aus.

Diese Version ersetzt Version 1.0. Die wichtigsten Änderungen betreffen den Erneuerungszyklus, den Rückgabeprozess und den Umgang mit Verlusten. Wenn Sie nach dem Lesen dieser Richtlinie Fragen haben, wenden Sie sich bitte an Workplace & Operations oder Ihre Führungskraft.

3. Process

The process follows the order below. Some steps run in parallel, and some require coordination between teams — the checklist is designed so that nothing depends on a single person remembering everything.

Step one: notification and kickoff. When People & Culture learns of a departure, they open an offboarding record and notify the manager, Platform & Infrastructure, Finance, and Workplace & Operations. The manager schedules a conversation with the departing employee to discuss the timeline, the handover, and any open questions.

Step two: handover planning. The manager works with the departing employee to identify ongoing work, open client engagements, and recurring responsibilities. A handover document is prepared, naming the colleagues who will take over each area. This document is shared with the receiving team before the final working day.

Step three: access and accounts. Platform & Infrastructure revokes access according to the timeline in §4 and the rules in POL-023. This includes system accounts, internal tools, and any

client-facing credentials. Access revocation for cause is handled separately — see POL-023 §4, which is manager-only.

Step four: equipment and property. The departing employee returns company equipment and any other property. Workplace & Operations coordinates this for office-based colleagues; for remote colleagues, a shipping arrangement is made. The return deadline is set out in POL-006 §5.

Step five: knowledge and documentation. The departing employee ensures that their documentation is current, that code and configuration notes are stored in the usual places, and that the handover document reflects reality. Managers should review this together with the leaver.

Step six: people and culture touchpoints. People & Culture conducts an exit conversation, if the employee wishes. This is an opportunity to share feedback in a constructive way. The departing employee also receives information about their final payslip, benefits, and any continuing obligations.

Step seven: closure. Once all steps are complete, People & Culture confirms closure with the manager and the relevant teams. The offboarding record is archived in line with our data retention practices.

7. Questions

If you have questions about this policy, please contact Workplace & Operations at people@kranich.example or reach out to your manager. For technical issues with your equipment, contact it-help@kranich.example. For questions about the financial treatment of lost or damaged hardware, contact Finance.

We review this policy regularly. The next review is planned for the coming year. If you have suggestions for improvement, please share them with the Head of Workplace & Operations, Rui Almeida. Related policies are the expense policy (POL-004) and the travel and reimbursement rates document (FIN-RATES-2026). Please refer to those documents for questions about costs that are not covered here.

Lost or Stolen Device Runbook

1. Purpose

This runbook explains what to do when a Kranich-issued laptop or mobile device is lost or stolen. Acting quickly protects company data and helps us get you back to work with minimal disruption. You do not need to wait for approval from your manager or team lead before following the steps below.

This runbook applies to all Kranich employees, regardless of where you work. Whether you are in the Ritterstraße office, the Rua do Alecrim office, or working remotely from home, the same process applies.

2. Report

As soon as you realise a device is missing, report it through the appropriate channel. If you believe the device was stolen, also report the incident to local law enforcement in your country of employment. A police report is not required to start our internal process, but it helps with insurance and any follow-up investigation.

You must report a lost or stolen device within 4 hours of realising it is missing. Do not spend time searching first; report promptly and continue searching while we work with you.

To report, send an email to security@kranich.example and copy it-help@kranich.example. In your message, include:

•  Your name and team •  The device type and model •  Where you last had it •  Whether you believe it was lost or stolen

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, realises her laptop is missing after a client meeting at a café. She sends the report email from her phone within the hour, describing the café and the time she last used the device.

context_blocks.header: [21] SEC-RB-LOSTDEVICE.pdf — Lost or Stolen Device Runbook > 3. Remote wipe (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Remote wipe

After you submit your report, the Information Security team will begin a remote wipe of the device. This erases company data and revokes access to Kranich systems. The wipe starts as soon as we confirm the device is missing; you do not need to wait.

If you have a company phone, it will be wiped too. Your personal data on that phone cannot be recovered after the wipe, so please note that anything stored locally will be lost. If you used the device for multi-factor authentication, the wipe will also remove those credentials. You will need to re-enrol a new device using 1Password and any other authentication tools you normally use.

While the wipe is in progress, do not attempt to log in to any Kranich service from the missing device, even if you think you have found it. If you find the device before the wipe completes, contact security@kranich.example immediately to stop the process if possible.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer working with clients in Poland, has his work tablet stolen from a rental car. He reports it within a few hours, and Security initiates the wipe while he files a police report.

context_blocks.header: [22] SEC-RB-LOSTDEVICE.pdf — Lost or Stolen Device Runbook > 5. Questions (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
5. Questions

If you have questions about this runbook or about a specific incident, contact the Information Security team at security@kranich.example. For questions about your Kranich device, hardware, or software access, contact it-help@kranich.example.

For questions about travel or booking a desk or meeting room at either office while you wait for a replacement, contact people@kranich.example or use Perch to book a workspace.

If your device was stolen while you were travelling for work, your manager should also notify the Workplace & Operations team led by Rui Almeida, so they can review any travel-related coverage under our internal policies. Refer to FIN-RATES-2026 for questions about expense claims related to the incident, such as replacing a lock or a bag.

Remember: the most important thing is to report promptly. Do not worry about blame or paperwork. Losing a device happens, and our process is designed to get you secure and productive again with as little friction as possible.

context_blocks.text:
5. Returning to work

When you are ready to return, please let your manager know in advance — ideally a few days before your planned return date. This gives your team time to prepare and ensures you have a smooth re-entry.

You do not need to provide a doctor's clearance to return unless your absence was long or your doctor recommended a phased return. If a phased return is appropriate — for example, starting with reduced hours or lighter duties — please discuss this with your manager and People & Culture. We will do our best to accommodate a gradual transition that supports your recovery.

If your absence was related to a mental health condition, we encourage you to return at a pace that feels sustainable. You may also want to speak with your manager about any adjustments that would help you settle back in, such as a quieter workload for the first week or more frequent check-ins.

Example: Sofia, a product manager in Fleet Insights who works remotely from Spain, returns after a two-month absence. She agrees with her manager to start with half days for the first week. People & Culture coordinates with her to ensure her pay and benefits are correctly adjusted during the phased return.

After you return, your manager may schedule a short conversation to see how you are doing. This is not a performance review — it is simply a way to check that you feel supported and that any ongoing needs are addressed.

If you find that you need to take further time off shortly after returning, that is okay. Illness does not follow a schedule. Please follow the same notification process described in §2.

4. Patching Keeping software up to date is one of the most effective ways to protect against known vulnerabilities. This standard sets clear expectations for how quickly patches must be applied, and it applies to the operating system, browsers, productivity software, development tools, and any other software installed on company-managed devices. Critical patches are installed within 12 calendar days of release. This applies to patches that address vulnerabilities with a known exploit or that are rated critical by the software vendor. Our device management tool tracks patch status centrally, and it-help monitors compliance. If a critical patch cannot be applied within the required window — for example, because of a compatibility issue with a specialized tool — you must notify it-help promptly so they can track the exception and apply a compensating control. For non-critical patches, including routine operating system updates and feature releases, we expect them to be installed as soon as they are available, and no later than the next scheduled maintenance window. Automatic updates should remain enabled at all times. If you see a prompt to restart your device to complete an update, do not postpone it indefinitely — a restart takes only a few minutes and closes the window of exposure. Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, receives a notification that a critical security patch is available for her laptop's operating system. She is in the middle of a customer call, so she dismisses the reminder and continues working. Later that day, she sees a second reminder from the device management tool and restarts her laptop during her lunch break. The patch is installed well within the 12 calendar days window, and Deniz has not put any customer data at risk. Software that is no longer supported by its vendor — sometimes called end-of-life software — must not be installed on company devices. Unsupported software does not receive patches, which means it can never meet the requirements of this standard. If you need a piece of software that is no longer supported, discuss alternatives with your manager and it-help. In rare cases, an exception may be granted for a specific business need, but the exception must be documented and must include compensating controls. Patching applies to all devices, regardless of where you work.

context_blocks.header: [28] POL-023-v2.0.pdf — Access Control & Identity Policy > 3. Access reviews (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Access reviews

Access rights are reviewed every 4 months. The review is led by Information Security and involves each team's manager. The goal is to confirm that every active account still matches the person's current role and that no access has drifted beyond what least privilege allows.

During a review, managers go through the list of accounts and permissions for their team. They confirm who still needs what and flag anything that looks unusual. Information Security then acts on those flags, which may mean revoking access, changing a role, or asking the manager

for more context.

Example: Sofia, a product manager in Fleet Insights who works remotely from Spain, changed teams last year. Her access review caught that she still held a permission from her previous team on the internal analytics dashboard. The manager revoked it during the review cycle, and Sofia received a short note explaining the change.

Access reviews also cover service accounts and integrations. These are checked against the same least-privilege standard. Any service account that is no longer used is deactivated promptly. If you are a manager, you are responsible for responding to review requests within the window given in the review invitation. If you do not respond, Information Security will follow up with you directly.

3. Timelines

We understand that facilities issues can affect your comfort and productivity. Our team triages every request when it arrives and prioritises based on urgency.

Safety-related issues are addressed immediately. For other requests, you can expect an initial acknowledgement within a few business days. The time to resolution depends on the nature of

the issue and whether external contractors are needed. We will keep you informed of progress if a repair takes longer than expected.

For example, if Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, notices a faulty chair in a meeting room, she sends a facilities request with a photo. Rui's team acknowledges her request quickly and arranges for a replacement chair. If Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, reports that the air conditioning in her area is not working, the team may need to coordinate with an external service provider. Anna receives updates until the issue is resolved.

If you have not heard back within a reasonable time, please follow up on your original email thread. You can also reach out to Rui Almeida or any member of the Workplace & Operations team directly.

4. Questions

If you have questions about this policy or about facilities matters in general, please contact Workplace & Operations at it-help@kranich.example.

For questions about equipment purchases or budgets, please refer to the relevant finance policy. For questions about office access, security, or visitor management, please refer to POL-004. For questions about travel or booking office space in other locations, please refer to the applicable travel policy.

We encourage you to report issues early. Small problems are easier and faster to fix than large ones. Your observations help us keep our offices welcoming and safe for everyone. Thank you for helping us maintain a great working environment.

context_blocks.header: [30] SEC-RB-ACCESS.pdf — Access Requests Runbook > 3. Locked accounts (p. 1–2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Locked accounts

Accounts can become locked after several failed sign-in attempts. This happens to everyone at some point, and it is not a reflection on you.

If your account is locked, do not keep trying to sign in. Instead, contact it- help@kranich.example and let us know which system you are trying to reach. IT resets a locked account within 30 minutes during business hours. Outside business hours, the reset happens the next working day.

If you are locked out of 1Password and cannot reach the IT help alias, ask a teammate to submit a request on your behalf. They should mention your name and the system in the request.

Example: Deniz, a customer success manager in Berlin, was locked out of Ledgerly while submitting a travel expense on a Friday evening. She waited until Monday morning, contacted it-help@kranich.example, and her account was reset within 30 minutes.

4. Reviews

Access reviews happen on a regular schedule. Information Security coordinates these reviews with each team lead. During a review, the team lead goes through the list of people who have access to their team's systems and confirms that each person still needs it.

You do not need to do anything for a routine review. Your manager will reach out if there is a question about your access.

Reviews also happen when someone changes roles. If you move from one team to another, your old team lead confirms that your previous access is no longer needed, and your new team lead confirms what you should receive. This happens in the background; you only need to submit the access request described in §2.

For systems with sensitive customer data, reviews are more frequent. The Fleet Insights team, for example, reviews access to customer telemetry data every quarter. Your team lead will let you know if your team follows a similar pattern.

If you notice that a former colleague still appears in a system, or that you have access to something you no longer use, let Information Security know. We would rather remove access too early than too late.

Doc Id: POL-006-v1.0 · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2023-02-01 · Owner: Workplace & Operations · Classification: internal

Equipment & Hardware Policy

1. Purpose

At Kranich Software GmbH, we believe that great work starts with the right tools. This policy explains how equipment is provided, maintained, and returned so that everyone — whether you sit in the Ritterstraße office, the Rua do Alecrim office, or work remotely from your home — has a consistent and productive setup.

We want the process to be simple and fair. This policy covers the standard equipment you receive when you join, how the budget works, when equipment is refreshed, and what happens when you leave or when something breaks. If you have questions that are not answered here, reach out to Workplace & Operations or write to it-help@kranich.example.

2. Standard setup

Your standard setup is chosen to match your role. For most employees, this includes a laptop, a monitor, a keyboard, a mouse, a headset, and a docking station. The exact models may vary depending on your team and your work. For example, a backend engineer in Routing Core may receive a more powerful laptop, while a customer success manager may receive a setup optimised for many video calls.

If you work from an office, your equipment is set up at your desk. If you work remotely, we ship the equipment to your home address. In both cases, the equipment remains the property of Kranich Software GmbH. You are responsible for taking reasonable care of it and for keeping it secure. Do not share your laptop or let others use it, even briefly.

Software is installed centrally by Platform & Infrastructure. If you need additional software for your role, submit a request through the usual channel. Peripherals beyond the standard setup — for example, a second monitor or a special chair — can be discussed with your manager and Workplace & Operations.

4. Timelines

How quickly should I submit? Promptly. The longer you wait, the harder it is to remember the business purpose and the more likely you are to lose a receipt. A good target is to submit within a few days of the expense.

What happens after I submit? Your report goes to your manager for approval, then to Finance for review. If something is missing or unclear, someone will reach out to you. You can track the status in Ledgerly at any time.

When will I be reimbursed? The deadline for reimbursement is set out in POL-004 §6. Reimbursement is paid through Ledgerly to your bank account. If you have not received payment by the time described in the policy, check the status in Ledgerly first, then contact Finance.

What if I submit late? Late submissions are handled case by case. The most important thing is to communicate: if you know you are behind, tell Finance. Silence is the only real problem.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, travels to Berlin for a planning week. She returns on a Friday and submits her report the following Monday. She attached all receipts as she went, so the report is complete. Finance processes it without any back-and-forth.

context_blocks.header: [33] POL-023-v1.0.pdf — Access Control & Identity Policy > 3. Access reviews (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
3. Access reviews

Access is not a one-time decision. People change roles, teams reorganize, and projects end. To keep access aligned with reality, we review access rights regularly.

Information Security coordinates an access review of all Kranich systems every 8 months. The review covers production systems, internal tools, code repositories, and administrative accounts. Each system owner receives a list of who holds access to their system. They confirm whether every person on that list still needs the access, and they flag anyone who should lose it.

Managers participate in the review for their direct reports. They confirm that the access their team members hold still matches what those people need for their current work. If someone changed teams within the last review period, the manager checks that old access was removed when the person moved.

The review is not a formality. When a system owner flags an access right as unneeded, we remove it promptly after the review closes. If a system owner does not respond to the review request, Information Security follows up. If there is still no response, we revoke the access rather than leave it in place.

Everyone plays a part between reviews, too. If you notice that you have access you no longer need, tell your manager. If you notice that a colleague has access that seems wrong for their role, tell Information Security. It is always better to ask than to stay silent.
