Doc Id: HR-003 · Version: 2.0 · Effective Date: 2025-01-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Performance Review Process

1. Purpose

Reviews at Kranich answer three questions: how did the last period go, where are you heading, and what support do you need. This document describes the cadence, the inputs, and what happens with the results — so the process is predictable rather than mysterious.

2. Cadence

Performance reviews run twice a year, in April and October. Each cycle takes about three weeks from self-review to the closing conversation. Between cycles, feedback stays continuous — the review is a summary, never a surprise.

3. The inputs

•  Self-review. You describe outcomes, not activity: what changed because of your work. Fern provides the (short) template. •  Peer feedback. You nominate two to four colleagues; your manager may add one. Peers answer three questions, fifteen minutes total. •  Manager assessment. Written against your role profile and the goals agreed in the previous cycle.

4. The conversation

The review conversation is an hour, held after you have read the written assessment — no live reveals. It ends with agreed goals for the next period and, where relevant, a development plan: skills, scope, or the path toward a role change.

5. Outcomes

Review outcomes feed the compensation round that follows each cycle; salary decisions are made by calibration across teams, not by individual managers alone. Promotions are proposed in the same calibration with written cases.

Example: Anna's case for senior engineer was written in October, calibrated in November, and effective in January — the timeline every promotion follows.

6. If the review is difficult

When performance is below expectations, the review says so plainly, together with a concrete support plan and a follow-up date. Nobody is managed out by silence at Kranich; that is a People & Culture commitment.

7. Probation check-ins

During the probation period, lighter check-ins replace the full cycle: end of month one with your

manager, mid-probation with People & Culture. The full review rhythm starts with the first regular cycle after confirmation.

Doc Id: POL-006 · Version: 2.2 · Effective Date: 2025-05-01 · Owner: IT & Workplace · Classification: internal

Equipment & Hardware Policy

1. Purpose

Good tools are cheaper than bad ergonomics. This policy defines what hardware Kranich provides, the budgets by role, and how ordering, refresh and returns work.

2. Standard setup

Every employee receives a company laptop plus the peripherals they need for a healthy setup — external monitor, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, headset, and a laptop stand. Home-office chairs and desks are supported within the budget below when your local setup needs them.

3. Budgets by role

The equipment budget covers everything beyond the laptop itself and renews with the refresh cycle.

| Role category | Budget | | --- | --- | | Standard role | €2,200 | | Engineering role | €2,800 |

Engineering covers software engineers, data engineers, and field solutions engineers — roles that routinely run heavy local workloads. Everyone else, including management, uses the standard budget.

4. Refresh cycle

Laptops and budget renew every 36 months. If your device struggles earlier — battery health, repairs piling up — IT swaps it without ceremony; the cycle is a guideline for planning, not a wall.

Example: Marek's field laptop lives a rough life in warehouses. When its hinge failed after two years, IT replaced the device the same week and simply restarted his cycle.

5. Ordering

Order through the IT catalog in Grove; anything in the catalog within your remaining budget is approved automatically. Items outside the catalog need a one-line justification to it- help@kranich.example — the answer usually arrives the same day.

6. Ownership and care

All equipment remains the property of Kranich Software. Treat it like your own: use the provided sleeve, keep liquids at a respectful distance, and report damage or loss to it- help@kranich.example immediately (a lost device is also a security incident — see POL-005).

Doc Id: POL-005 · Version: 4.1 · Effective Date: 2025-09-01 · Owner: Information Security · Classification: internal

IT & Information Security Policy

1. Purpose

Our customers trust us with the data that runs their logistics. This policy defines the security baseline every employee follows — devices, credentials, data handling, and what to do when something looks wrong. It is deliberately short; the point is that you actually read it.

2. Devices

Work happens on company-managed devices only. IT enrolls every laptop in device management before handover: full-disk encryption, automatic updates, and remote wipe are non-negotiable defaults. Personal devices may access the company calendar and chat, but never source code, customer data, or production systems.

Screens lock automatically after five minutes; lock yours manually whenever you step away, at home exactly as in a café.

3. Security training

Every new hire must complete the mandatory security training within 14 days of their start date. The training is assigned automatically in Fern on day one, takes about ninety minutes, and ends with a short quiz. Annual refreshers are assigned each autumn to everyone.

Managers can see completion status for their team in Fern; overdue trainings escalate to the Head of Information Security.

4. Passwords and authentication

Kranich provides 1Password to every employee, and using it is mandatory: every work credential lives in the company vault, no exceptions and no browser password stores. Multi- factor authentication is enforced on all company systems that support it. Never reuse a work password anywhere else.

Example: when Anna joined Routing Core, her first task was importing the team's shared service credentials into the correct 1Password vault — nothing is documented in wikis or chat.

5. Data handling

Customer data stays in production systems and approved analytics tools. Do not export customer datasets to laptops, personal cloud storage, or spreadsheets shared by link. Anonymized samples for debugging are created through the process described in the Internal Data Protection Policy (POL-010).

6. Network

The company VPN is required on any network you do not control — hotels, cafés, airports, and during workations. Home networks should use WPA2 or better with a non-default router

password.

Doc Id: POL-002 · Version: 2.0 · Effective Date: 2024-06-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Remote Work Policy

1. Purpose

Kranich Software is remote-first. This policy defines what "remote" means for us, what we expect from remote employees, and what you can expect from the company. Unlike the Workation Guideline (POL-003), this policy covers your permanent work setup in your country of employment — not temporary work from abroad.

2. Where you may work

You may work up to 100% remotely from anywhere within your country of employment — the country stated in your employment contract (Germany or Portugal). Working from another country, even briefly, is not covered here; see the Workation Guideline (POL-003) for temporary stays inside the EU/EEA.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, spends most weeks at home and books a desk in the Lisbon office through Perch when her team meets in person. Her setup needs no approval — it is the default.

3. Core collaboration hours

Teams agree on overlap windows rather than fixed office hours. The company-wide anchor is 11:00–15:00 CET: schedule meetings inside this window whenever possible, and keep your calendar honest about availability.

4. Workspace and equipment

Work from a safe, ergonomic setup. Equipment is provided under the Equipment & Hardware Policy (POL-006) — laptops, monitors and peripherals are ordered through IT, not expensed ad hoc. Kranich contributes to home-office essentials as described there.

5. Security expectations

Remote work does not relax security. Follow the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005): company-managed devices only, the company password manager for every credential, and locked screens whenever you step away. Public Wi-Fi requires the company VPN.

6. Communication defaults

Written first: decisions and outcomes belong in Grove or the team's project space, not only in chat. If a discussion runs longer than fifteen minutes in text, switch to a call — then write down the result.

Doc Id: POL-009 · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2023-05-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Code of Conduct

1. Why this exists

One hundred and forty people build Kranich together. This code describes the behavior we expect from everyone — employees, leadership, contractors, and guests at our events — so that "how we treat each other" never depends on who you ask.

2. The short version

Be professional, be kind, assume good intent, and speak up when something is off. Disagree with ideas as hard as you like; never with a person's dignity.

3. What we expect

- **Respect.** No harassment, discrimination, or demeaning behavior of any kind — in offices, remote channels, and at client sites alike.
- **Directness with care.** Feedback goes to the person first, in private, in a form you would accept yourself.
- **Reliability.** Commitments are kept or renegotiated early — silence is the only wrong option.
- **Inclusion.** Meetings and documents are written so a colleague from another team, timezone, or background can follow them.

4. What we do not tolerate

Harassment, bullying, retaliation against people who raise concerns, deliberate breaches of security or data-protection rules, and any behavior that would make a reasonable colleague feel unsafe. Alcohol at company events is fine; pressure to drink is not.

5. Conflicts of interest

Side projects are welcome as long as they do not compete with Kranich, use company resources, or crowd out your commitments. Financial interests in vendors, clients, or competitors are disclosed to People & Culture — disclosure protects you.

Example: Marek mentors at a local logistics-tech meetup that sometimes features Kranich clients. He disclosed it once in Fern; nobody has bothered him about it since, which is exactly the point.

6. Raising concerns

Talk to your manager, People & Culture, or — anonymously if you prefer — through the concern form in Grove. Every report is taken seriously, investigated confidentially, and retaliation is itself a violation of this code.

7. Consequences

Violations lead to consequences proportionate to the behavior, from a documented conversation up to termination. Deliberate breaches of the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005) or the Internal Data Protection Policy (POL-010) are handled under this section.

8. A living document

Suggest improvements in #people or to people@kranich.example. The code belongs to everyone who works here.

Doc Id: FIN-001 · Version: 2026-A · Effective Date: 2026-01-01 · Owner: Finance · Classification: internal

Expense Rates & Per-Diems

1. Purpose

This sheet is the single source of truth for per-diem rates and related expense figures. Policies such as the Travel & Expense Policy (POL-004) reference this document instead of quoting numbers, so that Finance can update rates once a year in exactly one place.

2. Per-diem rates by country

The full-day per-diem covers meals and incidentals for one calendar day of business travel.

| Country | Full-day rate | | --- | --- | | Germany (DE) | €28 | | Portugal (PT) | €24 | | France (FR) | €32 | | United Kingdom (UK) | €36 | | Poland (PL) | €22 | | Spain (ES) | €26 | | United States (US) | €55 |

Rates for destinations not listed here are set by Finance on request before the trip — write to finance@kranich.example with the destination and dates.

3. Partial travel days

For trips shorter than 8 hours, the per-diem is 50% of the country rate. Arrival and departure days of multi-day trips are treated the same way: each counts as a partial day at half rate.

Example: Deniz flies Berlin → Lisbon on Monday morning and returns Wednesday evening. Monday and Wednesday are partial days at half the Portuguese rate; Tuesday is a full day.

4. Meals provided by others

When a meal is already covered — a client dinner, a conference lunch, hotel breakfast included in the room rate — reduce the day's per-diem accordingly in Ledgerly: breakfast counts as 20%, lunch and dinner as 40% each. Ledgerly does the arithmetic for you when you tick the boxes.

5. Mileage

Using a private vehicle for a client visit requires prior manager approval and is reimbursed at the statutory rate of the country of employment. Public transport and trains remain the default.

6. Currency

All rates are stated in euros. Expenses paid in other currencies are converted by Ledgerly at the card provider's rate on the transaction date.

Doc Id: POL-010 · Version: 2.0 · Effective Date: 2025-03-01 · Owner: Information Security · Classification: internal

Internal Data Protection Policy

1. Purpose

Kranich processes two kinds of sensitive data: our customers' operational data (routes, depots, drivers' schedules) and our colleagues' personal data. This policy translates GDPR obligations into everyday rules that fit on one page of habits.

2. Ground rules

•  Purpose first. Personal data is used only for the purpose it was collected for. New purposes need a new assessment — ask the privacy team before building. •  Least access. You get access to the data your role needs, nothing more. Access reviews run quarterly per system owner. •  Shortest life. Data we no longer need is deleted on schedule, not "kept just in case". Retention schedules live in Grove.

3. Customer data

Customer operational data stays inside production systems and the approved analytics stack. Debugging with realistic data uses the anonymized-sample process: request a sample in Grove, and the platform team generates one with identifiers removed. Exporting raw customer data to laptops or personal storage is never acceptable (see also POL-005).

4. Employee data

Employee personal data lives in Fern with role-based access. Managers see what they operationally need — absence dates, not medical certificates; salary bands during reviews, not payroll files. People & Culture and payroll providers process the rest under contracts that mirror this policy.

5. Sharing with third parties

Any new vendor that touches personal data goes through the privacy review in Grove before a contract is signed: what data, what purpose, where processed, how deleted. The privacy team keeps the processing register current — if your tool is not in the register, it is not approved.

6. Data subject requests

Requests from customers' employees or our own colleagues (access, correction, deletion) go to privacy@kranich.example immediately. Statutory deadlines are short; never sit on such a request, even over a weekend.

Doc Id: POL-004 · Version: 3.0 · Effective Date: 2025-02-01 · Owner: Finance · Classification: internal

Travel & Expense Policy

1. Purpose

Business travel should be easy to do right. This policy covers when travel is justified, how to book it, what Kranich pays for, and how reimbursement works. It is owned by Finance; the warm tone is on purpose — the rules are few and firm.

2. When to travel

Travel when presence changes the outcome: client workshops, go-lives, team planning weeks, conferences you speak at. For everything else, default to a call. Your manager approves trips before booking.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer, travels to a logistics client near Kraków for a two- day rollout. His manager approved the trip in Fern the week before; nothing else was needed.

3. Booking

Book through Ledgerly's travel module using your corporate card where possible. Choose reasonable options: economy flights, standard hotel rooms, public transport over taxis where practical. Trains are preferred over flights for routes under five hours door to door.

4. Per-diems (daily allowances)

Kranich pays a per-diem for meals and incidentals on business trips. The current per-diem rates are maintained in the Expense Rates & Per-Diems sheet (FIN-001) — always check there rather than relying on numbers you remember, because Finance updates the sheet annually. FIN-001 also defines how partial travel days are treated.

Per-diems are paid automatically with your expense report; you do not need meal receipts for them.

5. What is reimbursable

•  Transport to, from and at the destination (flights, trains, local transit, reasonable taxis). •  Accommodation for the nights the trip requires. •  Client-related costs (a working lunch with a customer, printed materials). •  Roaming or a local SIM when your plan does not cover the destination.

Personal detours, minibar, and fines of any kind are not reimbursable.

Doc Id: HR-001 · Version: 3.0 · Effective Date: 2025-08-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Onboarding Guide

1. Welcome

Welcome to Kranich Software! This guide walks you through your first weeks — what arrives when, what to complete, and who helps. Your onboarding buddy and your manager have the same checklist, so nothing depends on you alone.

2. Before day one

IT ships your laptop and peripherals to arrive before your start date (see the Equipment & Hardware Policy, POL-006, for what is included). Fern sends you a link to complete your personal data, bank details, and emergency contact — ten minutes, best done early.

3. Your first day

Your manager and buddy greet you in a short kickoff call. You will activate your accounts, join the team channels, and get your 1Password vault access — from that moment, every credential you create lives there (POL-005 explains why this is non-negotiable).

4. Your first two weeks

•  Complete the mandatory security training — see §3 of the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005) for the deadline. The training is assigned to you in Fern automatically; do not postpone it, the deadline is firm. •  Meet the people your role touches: your buddy schedules five short intro calls. •  Read the policy starter pack in Grove: Remote Work (POL-002), Travel & Expense (POL-004), Code of Conduct (POL-009). •  Ship something small. Every team keeps a "first-week task" ready — Anna's was a one-line fix that removed a flaky test, and she still brings it up.

5. Your first three months

The probation period gives both sides room to check the fit; the terms and length are set in your employment contract and summarized in the Benefits Overview (HR-004) FAQ. Expect a structured check-in with your manager at the end of month one and a mid-probation conversation with People & Culture.

8. Practical FAQ

•  When does the probation period end? After 6 months from your start date; your contract states the exact date and Fern shows it. •  Where do I see my vacation balance? Fern, including carryover expiry dates. •  Who answers benefit questions? people@kranich.example, or your People partner named in Grove.

Example: Sofia used the wellness budget for a climbing-gym membership in Madrid and the learning budget for a product-analytics course — both approved in the same week, both in Ledgerly.

Offboarding Checklist

1. Purpose

Leaving well matters as much as starting well. This checklist covers what happens between a signed resignation (or a decided departure) and your last day — for you, your manager, and the back office.

2. As soon as the departure is confirmed

- People & Culture confirms your last working day and remaining vacation balance in writing.
- Your manager plans the handover: open tasks, owned systems, running client relationships.
- Fern generates your personal offboarding checklist — both you and your manager see the same list.

3. Your handover

Write the handover in Grove, not in private notes: what you own, where it lives, what is fragile, who takes over. Walk your successor (or your manager) through it in a call. Customer-facing colleagues introduce the new contact to clients before the last day.

4. Equipment return

Return all company equipment within 10 business days after your last working day. Remote employees receive a prepaid shipping label through the checklist in Fern; office-based colleagues hand everything to IT in person. The full list of what counts as equipment is in the Equipment & Hardware Policy (POL-006).

5. Access and accounts

IT disables accounts at the end of your last working day — this is automated from the Fern checklist, not something your manager has to remember. Shared credentials owned by your team are rotated; 1Password vault ownership transfers to your manager.

6. Money matters

Finance settles open expense reports with the final payroll. Untaken accrued vacation days are paid out as described in the Vacation & Leave Policy; overtaken days are deducted the same way.

7. The exit conversation

People & Culture invites you to a 30-minute exit conversation in your final week. It is optional and honest: what worked, what did not, what we should fix. Summaries are anonymized before leadership sees them.

8. Questions

people@kranich.example, or your People partner directly — every team has one named in Grove.

Doc Id: OPS-001 · Version: 1.5 · Effective Date: 2025-06-01 · Owner: Workplace & Operations · Classification: internal

Office & Meeting Room Guide

1. Purpose

How the Berlin and Lisbon offices actually work: getting in, booking rooms and desks, hosting guests, and the few house rules that keep shared space pleasant.

2. Locations and access

- **Berlin (HQ):** Ritterstraße 24, 10969 Berlin — floors 3 and 4. Access with your badge, workdays 07:00–21:00.
- **Lisbon:** Rua do Alecrim 12, 1200-017 Lisboa — floor 2. Same badge, same hours.

Lost badges go to it-help@kranich.example immediately (a lost badge is handled like a lost device).

3. Desks and rooms: Perch

Meeting rooms and desks are booked via the internal Perch tool — the mobile app or the panel next to each room. Two rules keep Perch honest:

- Each person may hold at most 3 recurring meeting-room slots; more recurring bookings require Workplace & Operations approval, which is rarely granted.
- Release what you will not use. Rooms free themselves after ten minutes of no-show, and repeat no-shows get a friendly note from Rui's team.

4. Hosting guests

Register visitors in Perch the day before: reception prints badges, and client visits get a room with the good coffee machine reserved automatically. Guests are accompanied at all times — office access rules exist for the same reason POL-005 does.

5. Focus and phone areas

Floor 3 in Berlin and the window row in Lisbon are quiet zones: no calls, no meetings at desks. Phone booths are first-come; calls longer than an hour belong in a booked room, not a booth.

6. Kitchen and shared spaces

The kitchen is everyone's: label what is yours, and the Friday fridge cleanup discards everything unlabeled. Team lunches can be charged per the Travel & Expense Policy when a client is present; otherwise the kitchen budget covers the basics — coffee, tea, fruit, oat milk included.

Doc Id: HR-004 · Version: 3.1 · Effective Date: 2026-01-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Benefits Overview

Everything Kranich offers beyond salary, in one place. Details and country specifics live in the linked policies; this overview is the map.

•  Wellness budget: €50 per month for anything that genuinely keeps you well — sports memberships, therapy co-pays, meditation apps, massage. Claim it in Ledgerly; no questions asked within the list in Grove. •  Statutory health insurance applies per your country of employment; People & Culture helps with provider paperwork on request.

Doc Id: POL-008 · Version: 2.1 · Effective Date: 2025-07-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Parental Leave Policy

1. Purpose

Becoming a parent should not require a law degree. This policy explains how parental leave works at Kranich Software on top of the statutory rules of your country of employment, and how we handle the practical side — handovers, pay, staying in touch, and coming back.

2. Scope

All permanent employees in Germany and Portugal. Statutory frameworks differ by country; Fern shows the rules that apply to your contract, and People & Culture walks every expecting parent through them personally.

3. Telling us

Tell People & Culture as early as you feel comfortable — earlier means better planning, but the timing is yours. The conversation is confidential until you decide otherwise. Your manager learns the dates when you are ready to plan the handover.

4. Leave and pay

Statutory parental leave and benefits apply in full. Where the statutory benefit replaces only part of your salary, Kranich tops up as described in the Benefits Overview (HR-004). The top- up requires no separate application; payroll applies it automatically once the leave is registered.

5. Before the leave

Plan the handover with your manager in the last weeks before leave: owned systems, running projects, client relationships. Example: when Sofia from Fleet Insights went on leave, her handover page in Grove became the team's template — one page, owners named, links to everything.

6. During the leave

You are a guest, not an employee-on-call: no meetings, no expectations. If you want to stay loosely in the loop, opt in to the monthly team digest in Fern. Company gatherings remain open to you, family included.

7. Returning to work

7.1 Planning the return

Agree the return date with People & Culture at least a month ahead so access, equipment and a re-onboarding buddy are ready. Ramp-up weeks with reduced meeting load are the default, not a favor.

context_blocks.header: [25] POL-005.pdf — IT & Information Security Policy > 7. Reporting security incidents (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
7. Reporting security incidents

If you suspect a security incident — a phishing click, a lost device, an odd login notification — report it to security@kranich.example within 24 hours of noticing it. Faster is better, and reporting a false alarm is always the right call. The response process itself is described in the Security Incident Response Runbook (SEC-001).

8. Enforcement

Deliberate circumvention of this policy is treated as a serious matter under the Code of Conduct (POL-009). Honest mistakes, promptly reported, are treated as learning opportunities — that is a promise from the Head of Information Security, Priya Nayar.

Doc Id: SEC-001 · Version: 1.3 · Effective Date: 2025-10-01 · Owner: Information Security · Classification: internal

Security Incident Response Runbook

1. Purpose

When something smells wrong — a phishing click, a lost laptop, an alert that will not explain itself — this runbook tells you exactly what to do, in order. It is written for every employee; the deeply technical playbooks used by the response team live separately in the security workspace.

2. What counts as an incident

Anything that could affect the confidentiality, integrity or availability of company or customer data. Typical examples: a clicked phishing link, credentials possibly exposed, a lost or stolen device, malware warnings, an unknown login notification, a vendor telling you they were breached. When unsure, treat it as an incident — false alarms are free.

3. Step one: report

Report a suspected security incident to security@kranich.example within 24 hours of noticing it — sooner is always better. One paragraph is enough: what you saw, when, on which device or system, and what you already did. Reporting is also the rule when the mistake was yours; a prompt report is explicitly a good look at Kranich, never a bad one.

4. Step two: contain what you safely can

•  Phishing click: disconnect from networks, leave the device on, report. •  Lost or stolen device: report immediately — remote wipe is triggered by IT; also rotate any credential you typed on that device recently. •  Suspicious login alert: change the affected password in 1Password and enable/verify MFA, then report.

Do not investigate on your own beyond this list — well-meant digging destroys evidence.

5. What happens next

The on-call responder from the security team acknowledges your report, classifies severity, and owns communication from there. You may be asked follow-up questions; incident channels are named #inc-… and are invite-only while the incident runs.

Example: when Deniz reported a convincing "shared invoice" phish that three people had received, the responder blocked the sender domain, checked click logs, and closed the incident the same afternoon — with a thank-you note in #security.

Doc Id: POL-003 · Version: 1.1 · Effective Date: 2025-01-15 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Workation Guideline

1. Purpose

A workation is a temporary stay abroad while you keep working — a few weeks near family, a month by the coast. Unlike the Remote Work Policy (POL-002), which governs your permanent setup in your country of employment, this guideline covers short-term work from another country.

2. What is allowed

You may work from other EU/EEA countries for up to 30 working days per calendar year in total. Both your manager and People & Culture must approve the stay before you book anything — approval covers team coverage on the manager's side and tax/social-security exposure on ours.

Days are counted per working day actually spent abroad, across all trips combined.

Example: Sofia, a product manager living in Madrid, spends three weeks in Portugal near her parents each spring. That uses 15 of her annual workation days, and her February request last year was approved within two days.

3. What is not covered

•  Stays outside the EU/EEA — these need a case-by-case review by People & Culture and are usually declined for tax reasons. •  Moving your work base permanently: a workation does not change your country of employment or your contract. •  Client-site travel — that is business travel under the Travel & Expense Policy (POL-004).

4. Your responsibilities while abroad

•  Keep your normal working hours agreed with your team, including the 11:00–15:00 CET anchor window. •  Follow the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005) exactly as at home: company device, VPN on untrusted networks, screen locked when away. •  Stay reachable: your emergency contact details in Fern must be current for the duration of the stay.

5. How to request

Request the stay in Fern at least two weeks before departure: destination country, dates, and a one-line coverage note. People & Culture confirms the tax side; your manager confirms coverage. You will get a single approval notification when both are done.

Doc Id: POL-001-v2 · Version: 2.3 · Effective Date: 2025-04-01 · Supersedes: POL-001 v1.0 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose and status

This policy explains how vacation works at Kranich Software: your entitlement, how to request time off, and what happens to unused days. This policy supersedes Vacation & Leave Policy v1.0 in its entirety. If you find an older copy floating around, the version with the later effective date — this one — wins.

2. Scope

All permanent employees of Kranich Software GmbH in Germany and Portugal, full-time and part-time (pro rata). Contractors and working students follow their individual agreements.

3. Annual entitlement

Every full-time employee receives 27 vacation days per calendar year, on top of the public holidays of their place of employment. Days accrue monthly from your first day.

Tenure is rewarded: you gain one additional day for every 2 full years of service, up to a total of 30 days per year. The bonus applies from the calendar year in which the anniversary falls.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, joined in 2021. In 2025 she has completed 4 full years of service, so her entitlement is 29 days.

4. Requesting vacation

Submit requests in Fern as early as possible; your manager approves them. Approval is the default — pushback happens only when critical coverage is at risk, and your manager will propose an alternative window.

For any absence longer than 5 consecutive working days, give at least 4 weeks of notice. Single days and short breaks are flexible.

5. Carryover

Unused days may be carried into the next calendar year and expire on March 31 of that year. We nudge everyone in January — carryover is a safety valve, not a savings account, and People & Culture reviews teams where large balances pile up.

Sick Leave & Medical Absence

1. Purpose

When you are ill, your only job is to get better. This policy explains how to report an absence, when a doctor's note is needed, and how longer illnesses are handled — with as little bureaucracy as we can legally manage.

2. Reporting an absence

Tell your manager and mark the absence in Fern before your working day would normally start, or as soon as you reasonably can. A one-line message is enough — you owe no diagnosis to anyone.

Example: Deniz woke up with a fever, sent "out sick today, moving my two calls" to her manager, and marked Fern from her phone. That is the entire expected process for a short absence.

3. When a doctor's note is required

A doctor's certificate is required from the 3rd calendar day of absence. Upload it to Fern; People & Culture handles the rest, including anything your health insurer needs. For absences of one or two calendar days, no certificate is needed.

If your country of employment has stricter statutory rules, the statutory rules win — Fern shows the correct requirement for your contract.

4. Sickness during vacation

Illness during booked vacation converts those days back to sick leave once the documentation above is provided. The vacation days return to your balance as described in the Vacation & Leave Policy.

5. Longer illnesses

From the second week onward, People & Culture stays in touch with you directly — about pay continuation rules in your country, insurer paperwork, and a return-to-work plan when you are ready. Your manager is only told what they operationally need: that you are out, and roughly until when.

6. Medical appointments

Routine appointments that must happen during working hours are simply worked around — block the calendar, no Fern entry needed. Recurring treatments are arranged individually and confidentially with People & Culture.

7. Privacy

Medical information is stored in Fern with access restricted to People & Culture. Managers never see diagnoses or certificates — only absence dates.

8. Questions

people@kranich.example, confidentially and any time.

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose

Rest matters. This policy explains how vacation works at Kranich Software: how many days you get, how to request them, and what happens to days you did not use. It is written for employees, not lawyers — when in doubt, ask People & Culture (people@kranich.example).

2. Scope

This policy applies to all permanent employees of Kranich Software GmbH in Germany and Portugal, full-time and part-time. Part-time entitlements are calculated pro rata. Contractors and working students have their terms defined in their individual agreements.

3. Annual entitlement

Every full-time employee receives 24 vacation days per calendar year, in addition to the public holidays of their place of employment. Days accrue monthly from your first day of work.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, joined on 1 July. In her first calendar year she accrues half of the annual entitlement.

4. Requesting vacation

Submit requests in Fern, ideally as early as you can. Your manager approves requests; they will only push back when critical team coverage is at risk, and will propose an alternative window when they do.

For any absence longer than 5 consecutive working days, please give at least 4 weeks of notice. Shorter absences are flexible — a same-week request for a single day is usually fine.

5. Carryover

We want you to actually take your vacation. Unused days may be carried into the next calendar year, but they expire on March 15 of that year. Days that are not used by then are forfeited. Plan winter and early-spring breaks accordingly.

6. Sickness during vacation

If you fall ill during booked vacation, the affected days are converted back to sick leave once you provide the documentation described in the Sick Leave & Medical Absence policy (POL-007). Notify your manager as soon as you reasonably can.

question: What share of a team can be rated 'exceeds expectations' in calibration?
expected_answer: At most 20% of a team's ratings
answer_text: No more than 20% of a team's ratings may be "exceeds expectations"; above that share, calibration requires separating genuinely exceptional outcomes from a strong year [1].

context_blocks.header: [1] HR-003.pdf — Performance Review Process > 9. Calibration guidance for managers (p. 2)
context_blocks.text:
9. Calibration guidance for managers

Access: Managers only

Calibration makes individual assessments consistent across teams. Each manager brings proposed ratings and a short written case per person; People & Culture chairs, and a manager from another team acts as challenger. The bar is the same everywhere.

To keep the top rating meaningful, no more than 20% of a team's ratings may be "exceeds expectations". Above that share, calibration will ask you to separate genuinely exceptional outcomes from a strong year — both are good news, but only the first is the top rating. There is no floor for the lower ratings; nobody is pushed down to fill a curve.

Example: Ines Duarte, engineering manager for Routing Core in Berlin, arrived with more top ratings than the share allows; after the discussion, the strongest cases kept it and the others received "meets expectations" with a note on what would make the difference next cycle. Proposed ratings stay confidential until the review conversation (see §4).

Doc Id: HR-003 · Version: 2.0 · Effective Date: 2025-01-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Performance Review Process

1. Purpose

Reviews at Kranich answer three questions: how did the last period go, where are you heading, and what support do you need. This document describes the cadence, the inputs, and what happens with the results — so the process is predictable rather than mysterious.

2. Cadence

Performance reviews run twice a year, in April and October. Each cycle takes about three weeks from self-review to the closing conversation. Between cycles, feedback stays continuous — the review is a summary, never a surprise.

3. The inputs

•  Self-review. You describe outcomes, not activity: what changed because of your work. Fern provides the (short) template. •  Peer feedback. You nominate two to four colleagues; your manager may add one. Peers answer three questions, fifteen minutes total. •  Manager assessment. Written against your role profile and the goals agreed in the previous cycle.

4. The conversation

The review conversation is an hour, held after you have read the written assessment — no live reveals. It ends with agreed goals for the next period and, where relevant, a development plan: skills, scope, or the path toward a role change.

5. Outcomes

Review outcomes feed the compensation round that follows each cycle; salary decisions are made by calibration across teams, not by individual managers alone. Promotions are proposed in the same calibration with written cases.

Example: Anna's case for senior engineer was written in October, calibrated in November, and effective in January — the timeline every promotion follows.

6. If the review is difficult

When performance is below expectations, the review says so plainly, together with a concrete support plan and a follow-up date. Nobody is managed out by silence at Kranich; that is a People & Culture commitment.

7. Probation check-ins

During the probation period, lighter check-ins replace the full cycle: end of month one with your

manager, mid-probation with People & Culture. The full review rhythm starts with the first regular cycle after confirmation.

Doc Id: POL-006 · Version: 2.2 · Effective Date: 2025-05-01 · Owner: IT & Workplace · Classification: internal

Equipment & Hardware Policy

1. Purpose

Good tools are cheaper than bad ergonomics. This policy defines what hardware Kranich provides, the budgets by role, and how ordering, refresh and returns work.

2. Standard setup

Every employee receives a company laptop plus the peripherals they need for a healthy setup — external monitor, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, headset, and a laptop stand. Home-office chairs and desks are supported within the budget below when your local setup needs them.

3. Budgets by role

The equipment budget covers everything beyond the laptop itself and renews with the refresh cycle.

| Role category | Budget | | --- | --- | | Standard role | €2,200 | | Engineering role | €2,800 |

Engineering covers software engineers, data engineers, and field solutions engineers — roles that routinely run heavy local workloads. Everyone else, including management, uses the standard budget.

4. Refresh cycle

Laptops and budget renew every 36 months. If your device struggles earlier — battery health, repairs piling up — IT swaps it without ceremony; the cycle is a guideline for planning, not a wall.

Example: Marek's field laptop lives a rough life in warehouses. When its hinge failed after two years, IT replaced the device the same week and simply restarted his cycle.

5. Ordering

Order through the IT catalog in Grove; anything in the catalog within your remaining budget is approved automatically. Items outside the catalog need a one-line justification to it- help@kranich.example — the answer usually arrives the same day.

6. Ownership and care

All equipment remains the property of Kranich Software. Treat it like your own: use the provided sleeve, keep liquids at a respectful distance, and report damage or loss to it- help@kranich.example immediately (a lost device is also a security incident — see POL-005).

Doc Id: POL-005 · Version: 4.1 · Effective Date: 2025-09-01 · Owner: Information Security · Classification: internal

IT & Information Security Policy

1. Purpose

Our customers trust us with the data that runs their logistics. This policy defines the security baseline every employee follows — devices, credentials, data handling, and what to do when something looks wrong. It is deliberately short; the point is that you actually read it.

2. Devices

Work happens on company-managed devices only. IT enrolls every laptop in device management before handover: full-disk encryption, automatic updates, and remote wipe are non-negotiable defaults. Personal devices may access the company calendar and chat, but never source code, customer data, or production systems.

Screens lock automatically after five minutes; lock yours manually whenever you step away, at home exactly as in a café.

3. Security training

Every new hire must complete the mandatory security training within 14 days of their start date. The training is assigned automatically in Fern on day one, takes about ninety minutes, and ends with a short quiz. Annual refreshers are assigned each autumn to everyone.

Managers can see completion status for their team in Fern; overdue trainings escalate to the Head of Information Security.

4. Passwords and authentication

Kranich provides 1Password to every employee, and using it is mandatory: every work credential lives in the company vault, no exceptions and no browser password stores. Multi- factor authentication is enforced on all company systems that support it. Never reuse a work password anywhere else.

Example: when Anna joined Routing Core, her first task was importing the team's shared service credentials into the correct 1Password vault — nothing is documented in wikis or chat.

5. Data handling

Customer data stays in production systems and approved analytics tools. Do not export customer datasets to laptops, personal cloud storage, or spreadsheets shared by link. Anonymized samples for debugging are created through the process described in the Internal Data Protection Policy (POL-010).

6. Network

The company VPN is required on any network you do not control — hotels, cafés, airports, and during workations. Home networks should use WPA2 or better with a non-default router

password.

Doc Id: POL-002 · Version: 2.0 · Effective Date: 2024-06-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Remote Work Policy

1. Purpose

Kranich Software is remote-first. This policy defines what "remote" means for us, what we expect from remote employees, and what you can expect from the company. Unlike the Workation Guideline (POL-003), this policy covers your permanent work setup in your country of employment — not temporary work from abroad.

2. Where you may work

You may work up to 100% remotely from anywhere within your country of employment — the country stated in your employment contract (Germany or Portugal). Working from another country, even briefly, is not covered here; see the Workation Guideline (POL-003) for temporary stays inside the EU/EEA.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, spends most weeks at home and books a desk in the Lisbon office through Perch when her team meets in person. Her setup needs no approval — it is the default.

3. Core collaboration hours

Teams agree on overlap windows rather than fixed office hours. The company-wide anchor is 11:00–15:00 CET: schedule meetings inside this window whenever possible, and keep your calendar honest about availability.

4. Workspace and equipment

Work from a safe, ergonomic setup. Equipment is provided under the Equipment & Hardware Policy (POL-006) — laptops, monitors and peripherals are ordered through IT, not expensed ad hoc. Kranich contributes to home-office essentials as described there.

5. Security expectations

Remote work does not relax security. Follow the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005): company-managed devices only, the company password manager for every credential, and locked screens whenever you step away. Public Wi-Fi requires the company VPN.

6. Communication defaults

Written first: decisions and outcomes belong in Grove or the team's project space, not only in chat. If a discussion runs longer than fifteen minutes in text, switch to a call — then write down the result.

Doc Id: POL-009 · Version: 1.0 · Effective Date: 2023-05-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Code of Conduct

1. Why this exists

One hundred and forty people build Kranich together. This code describes the behavior we expect from everyone — employees, leadership, contractors, and guests at our events — so that "how we treat each other" never depends on who you ask.

2. The short version

Be professional, be kind, assume good intent, and speak up when something is off. Disagree with ideas as hard as you like; never with a person's dignity.

3. What we expect

- **Respect.** No harassment, discrimination, or demeaning behavior of any kind — in offices, remote channels, and at client sites alike.
- **Directness with care.** Feedback goes to the person first, in private, in a form you would accept yourself.
- **Reliability.** Commitments are kept or renegotiated early — silence is the only wrong option.
- **Inclusion.** Meetings and documents are written so a colleague from another team, timezone, or background can follow them.

4. What we do not tolerate

Harassment, bullying, retaliation against people who raise concerns, deliberate breaches of security or data-protection rules, and any behavior that would make a reasonable colleague feel unsafe. Alcohol at company events is fine; pressure to drink is not.

5. Conflicts of interest

Side projects are welcome as long as they do not compete with Kranich, use company resources, or crowd out your commitments. Financial interests in vendors, clients, or competitors are disclosed to People & Culture — disclosure protects you.

Example: Marek mentors at a local logistics-tech meetup that sometimes features Kranich clients. He disclosed it once in Fern; nobody has bothered him about it since, which is exactly the point.

6. Raising concerns

Talk to your manager, People & Culture, or — anonymously if you prefer — through the concern form in Grove. Every report is taken seriously, investigated confidentially, and retaliation is itself a violation of this code.

7. Consequences

Violations lead to consequences proportionate to the behavior, from a documented conversation up to termination. Deliberate breaches of the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005) or the Internal Data Protection Policy (POL-010) are handled under this section.

8. A living document

Suggest improvements in #people or to people@kranich.example. The code belongs to everyone who works here.

Doc Id: FIN-001 · Version: 2026-A · Effective Date: 2026-01-01 · Owner: Finance · Classification: internal

Expense Rates & Per-Diems

1. Purpose

This sheet is the single source of truth for per-diem rates and related expense figures. Policies such as the Travel & Expense Policy (POL-004) reference this document instead of quoting numbers, so that Finance can update rates once a year in exactly one place.

2. Per-diem rates by country

The full-day per-diem covers meals and incidentals for one calendar day of business travel.

| Country | Full-day rate | | --- | --- | | Germany (DE) | €28 | | Portugal (PT) | €24 | | France (FR) | €32 | | United Kingdom (UK) | €36 | | Poland (PL) | €22 | | Spain (ES) | €26 | | United States (US) | €55 |

Rates for destinations not listed here are set by Finance on request before the trip — write to finance@kranich.example with the destination and dates.

3. Partial travel days

For trips shorter than 8 hours, the per-diem is 50% of the country rate. Arrival and departure days of multi-day trips are treated the same way: each counts as a partial day at half rate.

Example: Deniz flies Berlin → Lisbon on Monday morning and returns Wednesday evening. Monday and Wednesday are partial days at half the Portuguese rate; Tuesday is a full day.

4. Meals provided by others

When a meal is already covered — a client dinner, a conference lunch, hotel breakfast included in the room rate — reduce the day's per-diem accordingly in Ledgerly: breakfast counts as 20%, lunch and dinner as 40% each. Ledgerly does the arithmetic for you when you tick the boxes.

5. Mileage

Using a private vehicle for a client visit requires prior manager approval and is reimbursed at the statutory rate of the country of employment. Public transport and trains remain the default.

6. Currency

All rates are stated in euros. Expenses paid in other currencies are converted by Ledgerly at the card provider's rate on the transaction date.

9. Manager checklist for departures for cause

Access: Managers only

Most departures follow the checklist above. A departure for cause — termination without notice after serious misconduct — runs differently. Involve your People partner first: they confirm the legal basis and prepare the conversation with you.

On the day, hold the conversation with a People & Culture colleague present, collect the laptop and any hardware tokens, and notify IT immediately via it-help@kranich.example with the words "departure for cause". The automated deactivation from Fern is too slow here; a normal departure keeps access until the end of the last working day (see §5).

Afterwards, rotate shared credentials and inform the team factually, without detail. Example: Ines Duarte, engineering manager in Berlin, kept a private note of the timeline — notification sent, access revoked, credentials rotated — which People & Culture later needed for the file.

Doc Id: POL-010 · Version: 2.0 · Effective Date: 2025-03-01 · Owner: Information Security · Classification: internal

Internal Data Protection Policy

1. Purpose

Kranich processes two kinds of sensitive data: our customers' operational data (routes, depots, drivers' schedules) and our colleagues' personal data. This policy translates GDPR obligations into everyday rules that fit on one page of habits.

2. Ground rules

•  Purpose first. Personal data is used only for the purpose it was collected for. New purposes need a new assessment — ask the privacy team before building. •  Least access. You get access to the data your role needs, nothing more. Access reviews run quarterly per system owner. •  Shortest life. Data we no longer need is deleted on schedule, not "kept just in case". Retention schedules live in Grove.

3. Customer data

Customer operational data stays inside production systems and the approved analytics stack. Debugging with realistic data uses the anonymized-sample process: request a sample in Grove, and the platform team generates one with identifiers removed. Exporting raw customer data to laptops or personal storage is never acceptable (see also POL-005).

4. Employee data

Employee personal data lives in Fern with role-based access. Managers see what they operationally need — absence dates, not medical certificates; salary bands during reviews, not payroll files. People & Culture and payroll providers process the rest under contracts that mirror this policy.

5. Sharing with third parties

Any new vendor that touches personal data goes through the privacy review in Grove before a contract is signed: what data, what purpose, where processed, how deleted. The privacy team keeps the processing register current — if your tool is not in the register, it is not approved.

6. Data subject requests

Requests from customers' employees or our own colleagues (access, correction, deletion) go to privacy@kranich.example immediately. Statutory deadlines are short; never sit on such a request, even over a weekend.

Doc Id: POL-004 · Version: 3.0 · Effective Date: 2025-02-01 · Owner: Finance · Classification: internal

Travel & Expense Policy

1. Purpose

Business travel should be easy to do right. This policy covers when travel is justified, how to book it, what Kranich pays for, and how reimbursement works. It is owned by Finance; the warm tone is on purpose — the rules are few and firm.

2. When to travel

Travel when presence changes the outcome: client workshops, go-lives, team planning weeks, conferences you speak at. For everything else, default to a call. Your manager approves trips before booking.

Example: Marek, a field solutions engineer, travels to a logistics client near Kraków for a two- day rollout. His manager approved the trip in Fern the week before; nothing else was needed.

3. Booking

Book through Ledgerly's travel module using your corporate card where possible. Choose reasonable options: economy flights, standard hotel rooms, public transport over taxis where practical. Trains are preferred over flights for routes under five hours door to door.

4. Per-diems (daily allowances)

Kranich pays a per-diem for meals and incidentals on business trips. The current per-diem rates are maintained in the Expense Rates & Per-Diems sheet (FIN-001) — always check there rather than relying on numbers you remember, because Finance updates the sheet annually. FIN-001 also defines how partial travel days are treated.

Per-diems are paid automatically with your expense report; you do not need meal receipts for them.

5. What is reimbursable

•  Transport to, from and at the destination (flights, trains, local transit, reasonable taxis). •  Accommodation for the nights the trip requires. •  Client-related costs (a working lunch with a customer, printed materials). •  Roaming or a local SIM when your plan does not cover the destination.

Personal detours, minibar, and fines of any kind are not reimbursable.

Doc Id: HR-001 · Version: 3.0 · Effective Date: 2025-08-01 · Owner: People & Culture · Classification: internal

Onboarding Guide

1. Welcome

Welcome to Kranich Software! This guide walks you through your first weeks — what arrives when, what to complete, and who helps. Your onboarding buddy and your manager have the same checklist, so nothing depends on you alone.

2. Before day one

IT ships your laptop and peripherals to arrive before your start date (see the Equipment & Hardware Policy, POL-006, for what is included). Fern sends you a link to complete your personal data, bank details, and emergency contact — ten minutes, best done early.

3. Your first day

Your manager and buddy greet you in a short kickoff call. You will activate your accounts, join the team channels, and get your 1Password vault access — from that moment, every credential you create lives there (POL-005 explains why this is non-negotiable).

4. Your first two weeks

•  Complete the mandatory security training — see §3 of the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005) for the deadline. The training is assigned to you in Fern automatically; do not postpone it, the deadline is firm. •  Meet the people your role touches: your buddy schedules five short intro calls. •  Read the policy starter pack in Grove: Remote Work (POL-002), Travel & Expense (POL-004), Code of Conduct (POL-009). •  Ship something small. Every team keeps a "first-week task" ready — Anna's was a one-line fix that removed a flaky test, and she still brings it up.

5. Your first three months

The probation period gives both sides room to check the fit; the terms and length are set in your employment contract and summarized in the Benefits Overview (HR-004) FAQ. Expect a structured check-in with your manager at the end of month one and a mid-probation conversation with People & Culture.

8. Practical FAQ

•  When does the probation period end? After 6 months from your start date; your contract states the exact date and Fern shows it. •  Where do I see my vacation balance? Doc Id: SEC-001 · Version: 1.3 · Effective Date: 2025-10-01 · Owner: Information Security · Classification: internal

Security Incident Response Runbook

1. Purpose

When something smells wrong — a phishing click, a lost laptop, an alert that will not explain itself — this runbook tells you exactly what to do, in order. It is written for every employee; the deeply technical playbooks used by the response team live separately in the security workspace.

2. What counts as an incident

Anything that could affect the confidentiality, integrity or availability of company or customer data. Typical examples: a clicked phishing link, credentials possibly exposed, a lost or stolen device, malware warnings, an unknown login notification, a vendor telling you they were breached. When unsure, treat it as an incident — false alarms are free.

3. Step one: report

Report a suspected security incident to security@kranich.example within 24 hours of noticing it — sooner is always better. One paragraph is enough: what you saw, when, on which device or system, and what you already did. Reporting is also the rule when the mistake was yours; a prompt report is explicitly a good look at Kranich, never a bad one.

4. Step two: contain what you safely can

•  Phishing click: disconnect from networks, leave the device on, report. •  Lost or stolen device: report immediately — remote wipe is triggered by IT; also rotate any credential you typed on that device recently. •  Suspicious login alert: change the affected password in 1Password and enable/verify MFA, then report.

Do not investigate on your own beyond this list — well-meant digging destroys evidence.

5. What happens next

The on-call responder from the security team acknowledges your report, classifies severity, and owns communication from there. You may be asked follow-up questions; incident channels are named #inc-… and are invite-only while the incident runs.

Example: when Deniz reported a convincing "shared invoice" phish that three people had received, the responder blocked the sender domain, checked click logs, and closed the incident the same afternoon — with a thank-you note in #security.

Workation Guideline

1. Purpose

A workation is a temporary stay abroad while you keep working — a few weeks near family, a month by the coast. Unlike the Remote Work Policy (POL-002), which governs your permanent setup in your country of employment, this guideline covers short-term work from another country.

2. What is allowed

You may work from other EU/EEA countries for up to 30 working days per calendar year in total. Both your manager and People & Culture must approve the stay before you book anything — approval covers team coverage on the manager's side and tax/social-security exposure on ours.

Days are counted per working day actually spent abroad, across all trips combined.

Example: Sofia, a product manager living in Madrid, spends three weeks in Portugal near her parents each spring. That uses 15 of her annual workation days, and her February request last year was approved within two days.

3. What is not covered

•  Stays outside the EU/EEA — these need a case-by-case review by People & Culture and are usually declined for tax reasons. •  Moving your work base permanently: a workation does not change your country of employment or your contract. •  Client-site travel — that is business travel under the Travel & Expense Policy (POL-004).

4. Your responsibilities while abroad

•  Keep your normal working hours agreed with your team, including the 11:00–15:00 CET anchor window. •  Follow the IT & Information Security Policy (POL-005) exactly as at home: company device, VPN on untrusted networks, screen locked when away. •  Stay reachable: your emergency contact details in Fern must be current for the duration of the stay.

5. How to request

Request the stay in Fern at least two weeks before departure: destination country, dates, and a one-line coverage note. People & Culture confirms the tax side; your manager confirms coverage. You will get a single approval notification when both are done.

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose and status

This policy explains how vacation works at Kranich Software: your entitlement, how to request time off, and what happens to unused days. This policy supersedes Vacation & Leave Policy v1.0 in its entirety. If you find an older copy floating around, the version with the later effective date — this one — wins.

2. Scope

All permanent employees of Kranich Software GmbH in Germany and Portugal, full-time and part-time (pro rata). Contractors and working students follow their individual agreements.

3. Annual entitlement

Every full-time employee receives 27 vacation days per calendar year, on top of the public holidays of their place of employment. Days accrue monthly from your first day.

Tenure is rewarded: you gain one additional day for every 2 full years of service, up to a total of 30 days per year. The bonus applies from the calendar year in which the anniversary falls.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, joined in 2021. In 2025 she has completed 4 full years of service, so her entitlement is 29 days.

4. Requesting vacation

Submit requests in Fern as early as possible; your manager approves them. Approval is the default — pushback happens only when critical coverage is at risk, and your manager will propose an alternative window.

For any absence longer than 5 consecutive working days, give at least 4 weeks of notice. Single days and short breaks are flexible.

5. Carryover

Unused days may be carried into the next calendar year and expire on March 31 of that year. We nudge everyone in January — carryover is a safety valve, not a savings account, and People & Culture reviews teams where large balances pile up.

Sick Leave & Medical Absence

1. Purpose

When you are ill, your only job is to get better. This policy explains how to report an absence, when a doctor's note is needed, and how longer illnesses are handled — with as little bureaucracy as we can legally manage.

2. Reporting an absence

Tell your manager and mark the absence in Fern before your working day would normally start, or as soon as you reasonably can. A one-line message is enough — you owe no diagnosis to anyone.

Example: Deniz woke up with a fever, sent "out sick today, moving my two calls" to her manager, and marked Fern from her phone. That is the entire expected process for a short absence.

3. When a doctor's note is required

A doctor's certificate is required from the 3rd calendar day of absence. Upload it to Fern; People & Culture handles the rest, including anything your health insurer needs. For absences of one or two calendar days, no certificate is needed.

If your country of employment has stricter statutory rules, the statutory rules win — Fern shows the correct requirement for your contract.

4. Sickness during vacation

Illness during booked vacation converts those days back to sick leave once the documentation above is provided. The vacation days return to your balance as described in the Vacation & Leave Policy.

5. Longer illnesses

From the second week onward, People & Culture stays in touch with you directly — about pay continuation rules in your country, insurer paperwork, and a return-to-work plan when you are ready. Your manager is only told what they operationally need: that you are out, and roughly until when.

6. Medical appointments

Routine appointments that must happen during working hours are simply worked around — block the calendar, no Fern entry needed. Recurring treatments are arranged individually and confidentially with People & Culture.

7. Privacy

Medical information is stored in Fern with access restricted to People & Culture. Managers never see diagnoses or certificates — only absence dates.

8. Questions

people@kranich.example, confidentially and any time.

Vacation & Leave Policy

1. Purpose

Rest matters. This policy explains how vacation works at Kranich Software: how many days you get, how to request them, and what happens to days you did not use. It is written for employees, not lawyers — when in doubt, ask People & Culture (people@kranich.example).

2. Scope

This policy applies to all permanent employees of Kranich Software GmbH in Germany and Portugal, full-time and part-time. Part-time entitlements are calculated pro rata. Contractors and working students have their terms defined in their individual agreements.

3. Annual entitlement

Every full-time employee receives 24 vacation days per calendar year, in addition to the public holidays of their place of employment. Days accrue monthly from your first day of work.

Example: Anna, a backend engineer in Lisbon, joined on 1 July. In her first calendar year she accrues half of the annual entitlement.

4. Requesting vacation

Submit requests in Fern, ideally as early as you can. Your manager approves requests; they will only push back when critical team coverage is at risk, and will propose an alternative window when they do.

For any absence longer than 5 consecutive working days, please give at least 4 weeks of notice. Shorter absences are flexible — a same-week request for a single day is usually fine.

5. Carryover

We want you to actually take your vacation. Unused days may be carried into the next calendar year, but they expire on March 15 of that year. Days that are not used by then are forfeited. Plan winter and early-spring breaks accordingly.

6. Sickness during vacation

If you fall ill during booked vacation, the affected days are converted back to sick leave once you provide the documentation described in the Sick Leave & Medical Absence policy (POL-007). Notify your manager as soon as you reasonably can.
